subsubtopic: BURNING OF CANADIAN FLAG AFTER FILM FESTIVAL-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Last week the National Film Board, in Montreal, celebrated a film festival. It has been reported to me that at the end of the festivities a Canadian flag was burned in the yard of the National Film Board headquarters. In view of the seriousness of such a report, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn):
That the Secretary of State investigate this report to establish its validity and, if it is found to be true, investigate the circumstances, determine who was involved and report back to the House on his Findings.

speechtext:

In view of the fact that the leader of the opposition in the Quebec national assembly has come up with a reasonable suggestion to put an end to this dialogue which falls on deaf ears-the Ottawa and Quebec governments-concerning the sales tax issue, namely that both governments should sign an agreement whereby the federal government would collect the
$226 million and turn it over to the Quebec government, or grant a tax cut for the fiscal year 1978-79 which would allow the Quebec government to recuperate the sums involved, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the House urge the government to accept one of these solutions to put an end to the conflict between the Ottawa and Quebec governments concerning the sales tax issue.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED RAIL LINE ABANDONMENT IN MANITOBA-REQUEST FOR REVIEW-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the prairie rail action committee recommended the abandonment of the Quadra to Hamiota and Kenton to Wheatland rail lines in Manitoba, which the Hall commission said should be put under a prairie rail authority, and since the Canadian Transport Commission has acted with unseemly haste, without public hearings, to rubber-stamp this bad decision in spite of the assurance given by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to the House on May 4 that full hearings would be held, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton-Mel-ville (Mr. Nystrom):
That the Minister of Transport require the CTC to hold hearings to review its decision to abandon the Quadra to Hamiota and Kenton to Wheatland lines in Manitoba and to hold hearings on other PRAC abandonment recommendations, and that the Minister of Transport disband the prairie rail action committee and bring forward legislation to set up the prairie rail authority.

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Deputy Prime Minister. As the House knows, there has been considerable controversy in recent days about a potential conflict of interest involving members of this House. The basic problem is that there are no guidelines regarding conflict of interest for all members of parliament, and only meaningless guidelines for members of the cabinet.
Since the Prime Minister has said that conflict of interest legislation is ready, would the Deputy Prime Minister tell the House when we may expect to see this legislation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned I believe earlier in the week, the bill on the question of conflict of interest, or the independence of parliament, is ready. There are a few more points which have to be dealt with. It would be my intention, if possible, to bring the bill forward for first reading, if not in May then certainly in June. It would provide a basis for discussion of the whole question of conflict of interest as it applies to members of this House and to members of the Senate.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this legislation and we look forward to seeing it as soon as possible.
If I might turn now to the very difficult question of conflict of interest regulations as they apply to ministers-difficult because it is a question from which this government has backed away-on July 18, 1973, the Prime Minister said that the rules relative to members of the cabinet "will be put in the form of precise guidelines just as soon as parliament has had an opportunity to consider the green paper with regard to members of parliament and senators and the legislation that might be made applicable to them".
Parliament long since has considered that green paper. Will the Deputy Prime Minister tell us whether those precise guidelines promised nearly five years ago by the Prime Minister have been issued? If so, will they be made available to the House of Commons and to the public to see? If not, why have they not been issued as the Prime Minister undertook five years ago?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to check into the details and get more information on the question. But as I recollect it, based upon the statement that was made by the Prime Minister all ministers were asked to conform to a certain set of guidelines in handling their financial affairs with respect to their public duties. Certainly there has been communicated to members of the cabinet by the Prime Minister the obligations he expects ministers to follow with respect to conflict of interest.
I cannot answer the Leader of the Opposition as to whether these guidelines have been made public, but certainly the obligations which fall upon ministers have been communicated to them and ministers are expected to live up to those obligations.

Mr. Speaker, this is a matter of some concern because the Prime Minister went out of his way to make it clear that there would be, and I quote his words of July 18, 1973, "precise guidelines". Not some general directive, but precise guidelines. I presume that if those existed, the Deputy Prime Minister, as a member of the cabinet, would know something about them. I gather that since he does not, they do not.
I would like him to come back to the House of Commons and tell us if the undertaking of the Prime Minister regarding precise guidelines has been honoured; and I would like him, if it has been honoured, to table those guidelines. If it has not, I would like him to set an early date by which that undertaking will be honoured and to give us a commitment now that the guidelines will be tabled in the House of Commons. May we have that date? May we have that undertaking?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the Leader of the Opposition is mistaken in concluding that these precise guidelines do not exist. Precise guidelines do exist, they have been communicated to ministers and ministers have been expected to conform to the guidelines at the request of the Prime Minister. What the Leader of the Opposition is now asking is that these precise guidelines be made available to the public in the form in which they have been transmitted to the ministry: that is something I will check into further.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. It relates directly to the precise guidelines which, according to the minister, are available to members of the cabinet.
In view of the fact that the guidelines for cabinet ministers permitted a former minister of finance to take the so-called disclosure option, which involved disclosing the fact that he had a 30 per cent interest in a private investment company without disclosing the company's assets, does the government intend to close this loophole? I point out that when I first asked this question in November of 1974, the minister's predecessor took my question as notice and there has never been any answer to it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not have the details of the arrangements in the particular case to which the hon. member refers. Obviously, it is a matter which can be checked into, and I will do so. That is all I want to say on the subject.

Mr. Speaker, it seems that these guidelines are so stringent that members of the cabinet are held in terror by

May 25, 1978

them and are very much aware of them. Will the government amend the guidelines for cabinet ministers to require them to disclose their debts to outside creditors, as well as their assets? Also, will the government eliminate the loophole provided by the frozen trust option which allows ministers to manipulate public policy in full and private knowledge of the holdings in their frozen trusts? This is an option which has been followed by six ministers, including the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I think the allegations or suggestions made by the hon. member are quite unworthy, Mr. Speaker. The option available to ministers under the frozen trust option or arrangement does not permit manipulation of any kind. The hon. member should really revise his thinking if he is suggesting, as he seems to be, that public policy is being manipulated by ministers in order to accommodate the arrangements they have made under the frozen trust option.
If hon. members are aware of the theory of conflict of interest, they will realize that disclosure is one of the ways of dealing with potential cases of conflict of interest, and in the case of the trust to which the hon. member has referred, the option of disclosure has been used and is well accepted in dealing with cases of conflict of interest. The hon. member should not suggest that that is not the case.
I referred to the frozen trust, not disclosure.

Mr. Speaker, for the information of the Deputy Prime Minister and of the Leader of the Opposition, let me point out that the guidelines have indeed been made public. They were made public in a letter tabled by the Prime Minister which was written to the Deputy Prime Minister on October 18, 1976. It was tabled in the House on December 17.
My question to the Deputy Prime Minister is as follows: Given this government's discovery during the minority government days that such guidelines were essential, and considering that the Deputy Prime Minister promised in 1976 to act with urgency on the matter, will he, in assuring us that we will have the legislation in June, specifically promise the House that the following two aspects of the legislation in this area will be included in the bill: first, the legislation will establish certain moral and legal standards expected of all members of parliament in financial dealings; second, it will follow the successful British example of making it mandatory that all members of parliament declare their financial interests in a form which is accessible to the public?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for reminding us that the precise guidelines have been made public.

These are not precise guidelines.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
With respect to the independence of parliament legislation, the hon. member will recall that the green paper on conflict of interest was sent for study to an all-party committee of the House of Commons. That all-party committee has reported to a great extent; maybe not totally. We will be following the advice of the standing committee of the House which reported upon the proposals made in the green paper.
The hon. member will recall, with respect to the second part of his question, that the conclusion of the parliamentary committee is quite different from the request just made by the Leader of the NDP. Hon. members will be able to deal with the bill when it comes forward and see to what extent it has followed the advice of the all-party committee of the House.

Mr. Speaker, surely the minister can answer a straightforward question. He is quite correct in pointing out that what I am suggesting is different from the recommendations that came from the all-party committee-recommendations, on this detail, which my party did not support.
I should like to ask the minister precisely, given the very successful practice in the British parliament of making all ministers of the Crown declare, in a form which is accessible to the public, their financial holdings, will the Government of Canada now promise us that whatever else they may include in the bill, that provision will be there-because it is essential?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member may believe that provision to be essential: the fact is that the majority of the members of the committee decided otherwise. Normally, we are asked to pay more attention to the recommendations of parliamentary committees. Should we take their advice, or the advice of the Leader of the NDP?
Quite apart from that point, the bill will deal with disclosure provisions. It will be before the House of Commons and members from all parties will be able to decide what regime they wish to have followed in respect of how they deal with the very difficult question of conflict of interest. Hon. members know that there are other ways than through disclosure to deal with the question of conflict of interest. The House will want to consider what other options will be as useful as disclosure in the context of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, the minister is quite right; there are many ways of avoiding the problem which disclosure in this area is intended to solve. Given the answer of the Deputy Prime Minister, we can expect the bill not to include this very important provision. With respect to the second point in my first question, will the bill or bills the government intends to bring in next month also include guidelines which it thinks are appropriate for members on both sides, in terms of either moral or legal obligations which affect their financial dealings? I say this in the context of allegations which have been made, for example, by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce about behaviour on this side of the House, as

May 25, 1978
Oral Questions
well as the government side. Is that question to be dealt with by the government as well?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, certainly the interface between members of parliament, senators and, for example, the business community and what financial affairs will be tolerable, will be dealt with in the bill. We hope it will be dealt with fully. In addition to the written rules or the written laws which may be adopted by the House of Commons, there is a certain sense of ethics and responsibility which must be exercised by each individual member of the House of Commons. It seems to me that is a stronger guarantee, over-all, than to attempt to anticipate every possible situation which might cause a conflict of interest. I would add to the rules, regulations and the Standing Orders which may be proposed, the sense of ethics and responsibility that hon. members must follow in all their dealings: that is much more important.

Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I intended to address it to the Prime Minister, but he is not here. It is reported that the Prime Minister proposes to disclose, in a speech to the disarmament conference at the United Nations in New York, Canada's attitude toward the production of the neutron bomb.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is entirely appropriate that in a major speech on disarmament, the Prime Minister should include reference to this particular and quite important subject.
Why not to parliament?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no particular reason why not to parliament. I do not believe, however, that it would be possible to handle this question in the context of the question period: this is a most complex subject which I think it would be quite impossible to deal with properly.
I should like to make the observation that I have spent some five or six hours before the committee which includes members of all parties, and I think my colleague, the Minister of National Defence, has done the same thing; but I have yet to be asked a single question on the neutron bomb in the committee, where it would be possible to answer in full.
That is an evasion.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not consider it at all an evasion. speechtext:
The point I am making, regardless of legal distinctions, is that in terms of parliamentary decorum, in terms of gentlemanly behaviour on the floor of this House, there is no difference. Just as the hon. member for York-Simcoe apologized yesterday for what he had said, so, now, should the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce do likewise. It may be argued that the minister's assertions were made some weeks ago. But he repeated them yesterday on television.
My reason for feeling I have a question of privilege is that, as a person who does not belong to either of the parties which are engaged in this warfare, I am concerned about the image of parliament, and I suggest that these allegations back and forth between members of those two parties are not good for the image of this House. In these circumstances I believe I have a right to ask that just as one member yesterday did apologize, so there should be an apology from the other side.
It has been pointed out both in my questions on Tuesday and in the questions asked today by my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), that the heart of the matter is this: the picture is not clear. Members can make these charges of conflict of interest because no legislation is in effect against such conflicts. It therefore seems to me that for the good of the House there should be a cessation of charges regarding the financial operations of members and that we should clear up this issue. There should be precise legislation setting out the rights and obligations of members of parliament in their financial dealings, so that this whole situation can be cleared. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if you find I have a question of privilege, I would be prepared to move:
That the question of the urgent need for the introduction and passing of appropriate conflict of interest legislation to clear the air with respect to the rights and obligations of all members of parliament in relation to financial matters be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always believe in upholding parliament. I have a reference to make today in connection with a statement I made which is recorded at page 5628 of Hansard. Today two ministers, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), were unable to give answers because apparently the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has not yet told them what the policy he is going to enunciate will be.
The statement I made was this:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It arises out of the horrifying slaughter in Zaire over the weekend. At the present time, while there is no evidence that Cuban troops were engaged there, nonetheless 32,000- incidentally, transported to their destination by Air Canada-have been acting in such a way as to give leadership in undermining governments in Africa which would lead one to conclude that the leadership of Cuba has been taken over by others in this regard.
The statement I made was based on information from a reliable source who apparently misunderstood what the situation was with respect to the use of Air Canada aircraft. Two aircraft apparently were leased by Air Canada to Cuba under a lease agreement.
The information coming from this person, who knows the facts, was to the effect that Cuban soldiers were transported either directly or indirectly on these two aircraft. Today I tried again to get some information on the agreement. If the government has nothing to hide, why hide it? It is a very simple

agreement, according to the minister, who says he does not have possession, yet only the day before yesterday Air Canada stated that the documents were in the possession of the Department of Transport.
The statement I made was based on information which, as far as I was concerned, had always been acceptable. I made an error in the generality I used. This is my first opportunity to make it clear that, in so far as the Cuban troops now engaged in Africa are concerned, they were not transported by Air Canada. I have a high regard for Air Canada, but must say that a very serious mistake was made when it leased two jet aircraft to Cuba and, directly or indirectly, was beneficial to that country in its communist aggression with Soviet approval and support.

I will attempt to indicate as clearly as I can what I think a realistic package of business might be for the time between now and that date. Obviously I would like to clear all items from the order paper, and if hon. gentlemen would be generous they might indicate their willingness to do that, but in the absence of that generosity I will be realistic and indicate what I think might be achievable. If I am pessimistic, please correct me.
I have in mind two bills arising from the budget which are in the name of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien); the language of trials bill, which is in committee; the export development bill, which is also in committee; the bill in the name of the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) having to do with business reporting; the CALURA bill; and another bill which is in committee which has to do with the monitoring of petroleum corporations.
There is a notice on the notice paper today with respect to a bill in the name of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) having to do with disability pensions. That is also on my list. I discussed last week my interest in Bill C-28, and I noted the response I received when I raised that matter, but it still is very much on my mind. In addition, I would want to deal with a bill which will flow from the notice of ways and means which will be tabled today by the Minister of Finance. I mentioned that privately to representatives of the parties earlier today.
In addition, there is also a number of small bills which I have discussed with my colleagues and which might be dealt with as opportunities present themselves, and as Friday afternoons become available for these small items. I put it on the order paper as question No. 1,086 on January 23, 1978. All in all it has been approximately six months and nothing has been forthcoming. I think I am justified in raising this point. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a motion of which I gave Your Honour notice. I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), to move the adjournment of the House under the provisions of Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter which has been raised by many members for many weeks, which remains unresolved, and which now requires urgent consideration, namely, the withdrawal of railway boxcars from grain movement which, in spite of the provision of hopper cars by the government, is inhibiting seriously the efforts for record grain movements this crop year; the refusal of the ministry to implement the Hall Royal Commission recommendations regarding statutory Crowsnest grain rates and compensatory payments for the costs of transporting grain; the costs of demurrage charges for ships waiting to be loaded being assessed against prairie grain producers through no fault of theirs; the rail branch line abandonment recommendations by the Prairie Rail Action Committee that are counter to the recommendations of the Hall Royal Commission; and the lack of government legislation or responses to deal with these and other related matters and, which, as a result, prevents increasing our capacity to meet expanded grain export objectives.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   GRAIN SHORTAGE OF RAILWAY BOXCARS
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) gave the Chair the required notice pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 26. Having given notice of his intention to ask leave to move the adjournment of the House under the provisions of that Standing Order, he has now put forward basically the contents of that notice which in itself is in conformity with the provisions of the rule.
As is very often the case, I have no hesitation on this occasion in saying that these are very important and urgent matters raised by the hon. member. As he and other hon. members will understand, my decision must be made on the basis of the rules of precedent which confine me to the

question of urgency of debate, rather than the urgency attached to the particular subject matter. In this respect I must point out that this subject has been before the House in one way or another on a number of occasions, the most recent being April 25, 1978, approximately a month ago, on a motion on an allotted day which was critical of the transportation policy. That motion was by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski).
Subparagraph (d) of that motion called upon the House and the government to implement the major recommendations of the Hall commission report on grain handling and transportation in the west. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre moved an amendment to that motion, which read as follows:
(e) to reject the prairie rail action committee recommendations to close down the Liberty to Dilke and Eston to Lacadena rail lines, and to bring forward legislation to set up the prairie rail authority.
In the course of that day I am sure the hon. member had a great deal to say about the subject which he has put forward now. I take that only as a reference point to say that this and other occasions have already presented themselves.
A number of questions have been put forward during question period. It would seem to me, in the face of Standing Order 26(5), I am required to give some consideration to other opportunities for the discussion of these matters.
Also, I must make the general observation that we seem to be dealing with something which is more of a chronic rather than an acute matter in that it has been under consideration by the House for quite some time. Therefore it is not a proper subject for disposition under Standing Order 26.

The House resumed, from Wednesday, May 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-56, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to authorize payments related to provincial sales tax reductions, be read the second time and referred to the committee of the whole, and of the amendment (Mr. Broadbent) (p. 5548).

Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned last night at six o'clock, I had discussed the sales tax and the problems the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was having with his counterpart in the province of Quebec. Mr. Parizeau, the minister of finance for Quebec, seems to have come out of this encounter very well. He has outfoxed and outgunned the Minister of Finance in every category.
Let us look at what he has done. By selective tax cuts for those goods mainly consumed in Quebec and made in that province, in effect Mr. Parizeau has set up a non-tariff barrier.
May 25, 1978

That will not improve manufacturing in the rest of Canada and shipping into the province of Quebec nor garner any advantage. Presumably this will be directed to things like automobiles, wrenches, tools and so on. To this degree, in so far as sales tax is concerned, the province of Quebec has put its interests first, and in this it seems to have been eminently successful.
Each province received 2 per cent from the federal government in lieu of the federal treasury giving up 3 per cent. Each provincial treasury will lose that amount of money, but not the province of Quebec. That province will lose only the portion of money in its selective tax cuts, which is considerably less than the other provinces that went along with the plan. Even so, the Minister of Finance has seen fit to guarantee to the province of Quebec the same amount of money as if it had accepted the federal offer as did the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia.
The Minister of Finance showed that he bowed to pressure from Quebec, making payments that he should not have made if he was to be fair and intended to stick to what he originally attempted to do, and that was reduce sales tax right across the country. In fact the government of Quebec has been able to suggest it can have it both ways; it can have selected tax reductions but still be guaranteed the full value as though it had made a general 3 per cent tax reduction across the board. In the way this is being done the money paid to that province will come out of the general revenue of this country, yet the province of Quebec will maintain its own treasury and tax structure, without great losses. The Minister of Finance supposedly is a street fighter. All I can say in this regard is that he must have slipped on a banana peel when getting his gun out of its holster, because Mr. Parizeau really outgunned him on this occasion.
We are aware of the problems associated with the special status which some want for Quebec. The finance minister for that province has in this case been able to further the interests of his province without necessarily going along with what seemed to be in the national interest. If the Minister of Finance had stuck to the original idea of tax cuts he would have been much better off. He should not have acceded to the request of the finance minister for Quebec, that moneys be given that province indiscriminately.
I should now like to comment on the value of this sales tax reduction so far as its avowed intention of increasing consumer spending is concerned. I might suggest that Mr. Parizeau may have considered some of these things I intend to cover in suggesting that this tax cut will not do what it is supposed to do. It has been suggested there was a personal savings rate of 1114 per cent in the fourth quarter of 1977, which is twice as high as it has been in the past decade. This rise in the rate is considered by some to be the result of uncertainty over the political situation in Quebec and the possible rearrangement of the country.
Income Tax Act
There seems to be a trend to save and for people to be frugal. Personal savings have doubled at $45 billion compared to what they were five years ago. Investment in Canada Savings Bonds accounts for $18 billion. That is almost $2 billion more than last year. This money deposited in banks and invested in savings bonds is money not being spent for the purchase of goods and services. It is difficult to make this money available for investment in the maintenance of existing production, or in expansion or new production. The intent of this reduced sales tax should be to get the economy going and restore confidence.
Is much of the saving a desperate effort on the part of the people to conserve value by counting upon the earnings from the savings to offset the erosion of inflation? We also forget the extent to which savings are forced on the people. We have compulsory participation in pension plans, and because home ownership is so excessively subsidized there is a great deal of pressure on people to own houses rather than to rent. Indeed, a citizen loses out if he does not own. Housing has been used as a source of employment rather than as a means of housing the population.
Many people resort to registered home ownership savings plans because of the tax relief. We are putting some $2 billion into these plans, thereby depriving the government of taxes that have to be made up by other means. Incidentally, I think these registered retirement savings plans give too much of an advantage to people in the higher income brackets. Their savings are much greater and are really at the expense of the federal treasury. On the other hand, without this program, resentment against a regressive income tax would be much greater. It seems likely that much of the savings occur in circumstances that create government deficits, rather than contributing to productive growth.
How much of this increased savings is voluntary and how much is forced upon those seeking tax relief? This cannot really be measured. It is obvious that these registered retirement savings plans and savings bonds are designed to discourage liquidation, so the money involved is not really available for the purchase of goods and services in order to take advantage of a sales tax reduction.
In addition, one might ask what the implications of this increase in personal savings may be. How affluent are Canadians when the liabilities of the federal government alone have reached $51 billion and will increase by $12 billion in the next 12 months? These liabilities will have doubled in the last five years. It is obvious there has been a good deal of borrowing by provincial, municipal, and federal governments. They are borrowing in order to spend on social benefits. As a result, we are supplementing current income by borrowing on the future. If the borrowing were for capital goods and capital works, that would be another situation. Certainly the savings of many individuals are being discounted by the charges against them put on at various levels of government. Personal affluence may well be less than what we expect. This may be why the economy is not responding, as the experts have anticipated, to increased spending at both government and personal levels.

It is unfortunate that so much of this debate has been taken up in respect of sales tax, with complex abatements and rebatements, particularly when this represents only a minor part of the federal scene. I was astounded at a meeting of the Standing Committee on Finance the other day to hear Mr. Bouey of the Bank of Canada say that we had no real balance of payments problem. When the government has to borrow $3 billion on the foreign exchange market, with a line of credit for another $4 billion, costing us $100,000 a day, does that not mean our economy is in trouble? Surely Mr. Bouey cannot say we are in robust economic health when in fact we have had to shore up a floating dollar that is supposed to find its own level, keeping in mind the $11.5 billion deficit and the necessity to raise more money. All of this creates considerable problems for our economy.
Mr. Bouey said he would not monetize any of the government's deficits, except up to and within the limits of growth which can be set for the money supply. The money supply has already been growing too fast over the years. In the years from 1972 to 1974, when there was a minority government, the bank monetized some 66 per cent of federal requirements in borrowing, but that only amounted to a total of some $3 billion. Can the federal government in fact borrow $9 billion on the market this year to meet its financing requirements? Even if it is able to do so, how much will that leave the private sector? Without money in that private sector our productivity cannot be increased in order to provide the expansion in the number of jobs necessary to meet our growing labour force and increasing government expenditures.
It would be interesting to note what the Minister of Finance intends to do to resolve this difficulty. Will interest rates go up as competition increases for scare money, that is, competition to meet private and government needs? The minister has stated that the Bank of Canada will not inflate the money supply. Let me suggest that only by increasing interest rates can available capital be rationed.
There have been some events occurring around the world that are disturbing to the Canadian economy. Some are predicting a fairly severe economic setback early next year with the slowdown in the United States economy. The United States suffered a severe recession in 1974-75 when wage-prices were corrected. It seems likely that inflation will remain our greatest problem, and it is difficult to see, with the expected increase in inflation in the United States, how Canada can escape.
There are some good things in the budget, but some are more apparent than real. One is the expansion of the rollover provision for the corporate family farm. But unless what is interpreted as a rollover is more widely interpreted than the present regulations allow, this provision is not of much value. As we discussed in the House when the provisions were introduced in the last budget debate, the rollover provision applies only to like businesses, and in the interpretation of the Department of National Revenue, selling a dairy farm and buying a hog farm does not constitute a like business, nor does selling a grain farm and buying a cattle ranch.

These rollover provisions are not really of much practical value. They are really only of value where, for example, a farmer has a parcel of land farther away than he would like from his main operation, sells it, and replaces it with another. Unless the department is willing to expand the scope and to be more liberal in the interpretation of what is a like business, it has little value. In any case, of course, the capital gains tax must eventually be paid somewhere down the road, and in many instances it is probably better to pay capital gains tax rather than have it accumulate to be paid in one lump sum at the end of some generation when that generation leaves the farm.
The Royal Commission on Corporate Concentration had a few things to say about capital gains taxation. On the face of it there is a good argument to tax capital gains in fairness to tax on ordinary income, although presumably all capital gains should be taxed instead of half. But this principle has been eroded as it is realized that capital costs are an important and depressing problem to business. Obviously, the practical problem with capital gains is that it represents very often a great deal of inflation and that the savings of perhaps 20 years are suddenly to be taxed as if they were earned in one year, causing a loss to the extent that the capital gain is fairly well eaten up. As well, principal residences are exempted along with the first $1,000 of capital gains dividends and interest income, all of which have eroded the capital gains tax.
The problem is that for a very small amount of revenue, some one third of a percentage point, capital gains tax causes bad business decisions. People do not sell their businesses, real estate and so on because they find they will lose any gain that might accrue. Capital gains tax would have been fine if the economy had remained stable and with little inflation, but in large measure capital gains tax is only a tax on inflation as such and a great depressant to risk capital investment where the individual entrepreneur is concerned.
The royal commission had this to say:
The design of the capital gains tax ensured that it would do little in terms of equity and the most recent amendments to the tax law are a further step backward in this sense. The result is a complicated and costly addition to the tax system and a disincentive to business investment, with little compensating benefit.
I would certainly agree that the capital gains tax should be abolished. The enormous increase in government spending, particularly in social welfare programs in the past few years, has meant that the tax pay-out of federal and provincial governments has been enormously increased, and all our programs are not yet mature with such further things as bilingualism becoming more expensive. Furthermore, we are facing the probability of an attempt to establish some sort of guaranteed income for our citizens. This, I feel, would be certain disaster and would push our already overburdened service industry into more direct competition with that segment of the economy that produces our goods.
The minister mentioned that indexing of exemptions brackets since 1974 on personal income tax has meant that the take
May 25, 1978

is $5 billion below what it would have been in the absence of indexing. Specific personal tax cuts totalling $2.5 billion, and $1.6 billion for business, have reduced the federal tax take. Of course no one promises that without indexing there would not have been some alleviation in the tax structure. But with the government tending to increase spending at one end with maturation of programs and new programs, to have cut on the intake through the indexing system makes for fiscal deficit budgeting and conceals for a time the necessity of a better balance between income and outgo. Therefore I believe it is time to consider the fact of indexing and I believe governments must, instead of automatic indexing, consider whether or not they should make the proper adjustments in the rates and levels of taxation as they did in the past.
I know it is easy in an inflationary period to hide behind the index, but in fact it is now recognized the index is not a good method of measuring the total business activity. Studies in the United States have shown that indexing is probably fallacious and gives too high a figure for the cost of living index as related to the actual over-all business activity-something which is very difficult to measure, I know. It has been estimated that this cost of living is too high by something like at least 2 per cent, based upon what studies in the United States would indicate. It may well be that the present method of indexing is not as good a barometer as we would like to see.
I am inclined to feel that the use of indexing creates uncertainty and, while its intent is not questioned, it makes for difficulty in budgeting, and increases the incentive to borrow to cover deficits. I appreciate that more and more people in small business, and I presume in larger ones as well, make business decisions on how the tax changes and taxation system affect the business rather than attempting to run it on a careful and constructive basis. Rewards are as great by taking advantage of the tax system, rather than attempting to run an efficient business, and in the final analysis contributing jobs and economic activity to the over-all community. There are so many exemptions, indices and allowances that the tax accountant becomes the most important person in business management. I do not think this is a good thing.
I was pleased to see that the minister of small business has introduced some ideas and some intentions which hopefully will improve the climate for small business. There are a good many more things in the budget I would like to speak about, but at the moment I would like to wait for committee of the whole.

I am very pleased, Mr. Speaker, to have an opportunity to speak in this budget debate and on Bill C-56, which is perhaps one of the more important bills to be discussed in this House in quite some years. It is important not just because it is a budget bill, but because it is a specific budget bill, and also because of the nature of the debate that has surrounded the sales tax provisions.
There are two fundamental principles that must be examined. One of them is the relationship of a common market to a common market within a nation, and that total concept which has to be examined. The other has to do with how a nation like
Income Tax Act
Canada, in terms of global economics, mobilizes its resources, given the federal and provincial problems that surround confederation to meet some of these critical events that are occurring in our industrial world.
Before I deal with these two principles, I would like to review the sequence of events and the ideas that went into this particular budget and this particular sales tax proposal. We have had a great deal of discussion in the House about the difficulty in stimulating the economy and actually creating effective demand in it. We have had comments about the fact that the quantity or degree of savings in the country have increased immeasurably over the last 15 years. I believe in 1960 we had a savings ratio to gross national product of something like 2.3 per cent, and in the last quarter of 1977 it had risen to 11.25 per cent, which is more than a 400 per cent increase in the level of savings as a percentage of the gross national product. This is extremely substantial.
The effect of the tax cuts in last fall's mini-budget on purchases within Canada was minimal. It did not deter people from taking trips, but neither did it increase the demand for goods produced in this country. It therefore became important to find a method of stimulating the economy over a short period so that people would buy more goods. Most economists indicated that the reduction of sales tax would have a rapid effect.
The minister either met, or discussed this problem with all provincial premiers. The province of Alberta had no sales tax so it opted out, but opted instead for some concessions which favoured Syncrude and other operations in heavy oil and tar sands. That left nine provinces with sales tax. The minister was able to get agreement with eight provinces-not with the province of Quebec. The agreement with the five provinces from Ontario west concerned the transfer of 2 per cent to those provinces through the income tax after which the provinces would reduce the sales tax by 3 per cent, thus redistributing the federal funds by a reduction of sales tax. Because of the slack economy and relative poverty of the four Atlantic provinces, the agreement was for the federal government to fund the provinces for the full 3 per cent reduction in sales tax. The province of Quebec took part in the discussions but did not respond, and a few hours before the budget asked for an extension of 48 hours. I assume that if the budget had been delayed nothing would have been done.
Just 48 hours after the budget was tabled, the province of Quebec announced its program which called for an 8 per cent or total reduction of sales tax on specific items. These items are not totally made in Quebec, but in many ways this would create a separate tariff situation within that province for many of the goods produced there.
There is one aspect of all this which is not well understood, Mr. Speaker, and that is that in the other nine provinces the federal income tax and provincial income tax are collected by the federal government. In 1954 Quebec opted to collect its own income tax separate from the federal government. This

Income Tax Act
means that the operation could not be conducted the same way in Quebec as in the other provinces.
In the other provinces the federal tax would be reduced by $100 or the provincial tax increased by $100, and the money would be redistributed to the people. That is not possible in Quebec because there the people get separate tax forms.
Let us consider how this program could have operated under two sets of circumstances. Let us assume that the province of Quebec had gone along with the scheme. If it had, the full $226 million would have been sent out in the form of a cheque from the federal government and then redistributed to people in the province by way of a sales tax reduction. The province went along to the extent that there was some reduction on certain items, and for those items the two percentage point reduction will be transferred in this way. In other words, a cheque of roughly $40 million will be given to the province of Quebec to meet this particular reduction, but the other $186 million is not being given in this way because the province did not go along with the scheme.
In the other set of circumstances, the province does not go along with the scheme. If we give the province $40 million to make up for the sales tax being reduced by two percentage points, then the question arises of how we maintain equity in this country in terms of the people of Quebec receiving their fair share of this tax reduction.
Both the Tory party and the NDP have said we should hand over the full amount to the government of Quebec in the form of a cheque even though it has not gone along with the scheme, and then the province could redistribute it in a way that would favour its industry. I cannot accept this method, Mr. Speaker, because I think it would encourage a disruption of the notion of a common market.
The province of Quebec has every right, and should continue to have every right, to do what it wants with its own tax system. It is a different thing, however, when the federal government tries to do something and actually sends a cheque to do it or when the province does something that creates a kind of non-tariff barrier. This is extremely important. Two years ago the province of Ontario removed the sales tax on automobiles. That was a legitimate move. At no time, however, did the federal government offer encouragement to them to do that. This is the difference in the two situations.
I should like to deal with this notion of a common market, Mr. Speaker, because I have seen some things in the press which disturb me. The usual idea of a common market is that it is something that exists between countries and that therefore, in these circumstances we are not talking about the same thing. It seems to me that one of the essential things about nationhood is that the central government does everything it can to maintain the commonality of the market within a nation. This is the principle at stake in this issue. Should the federal government transfer $226 million to the province of Quebec to set up a tax system which tends to break down or disturb that common market-which tends to set up a nontariff barrier? Should the federal government be in that kind

of business? I say no, Mr. Speaker. I think this point is crucial and should be understood.
The other point I wanted to deal with, before I move on to some other aspects of our economy, is the nature of federal-provincial relationships, particularly in a very critical period in our economic history and in the world. There is a very basic difference between the position of the Tory party and the position of the government on this isue. Without putting any value on it, at this particular point it is unique, in the origins of this country and the origins of the Conservative party, that there is a different situation.
Speaker after speaker from the Conservative party has talked about provincial rights, stating that we must do absolutely nothing to reduce provincial rights. They never seem to think there are some very important federal rights that must be maintained. There is a substantial difference in viewpoint and this should be looked at very carefully by the Canadian public.
In this period of real crisis in our country and throughout the world, it is important that the federal government maintain as much power as possible to deal with the critical issues. When we begin making constitutional adjustments, which we are going to do, it is extremely important to remember that this country has a million unemployed, $11 billion deficit, S'A per cent inflation, and a foreign exchange deficit of perhaps $5 billion. This is not the time to dissipate the power of the federal government to deal with these problems.
When we are criticized in terms of this tax situation, I am afraid it creates the impression that we are in some way trying to usurp provincial powers. What the minister attempted to do, and it was extremely important, in my opinion, was to say that the provinces have a taxing power which we do not, and that we should get together with the provincial finance ministers. This did not start a few weeks before the budget. It began eight months to a year ago. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) asked them to sit down to see how co-operatively they could work out a system to reduce sales tax in order to create a demand to solve part of our problem.
It is extremely important that in a crisis situation, almost like a wartime situation, we have the collective support of the provinces. We need to work with the provinces. We need as much power as possible to solve some of these problems. I would like to deal briefly with the global nature of these problems. In dealing with this budget, we have to realize it is a short term instrument which will provide stimulation for a six to eight-month period. It is not a budget to deal with the global crisis that we face.
Let us take a country with an inflation rate of 16 per cent, an unemployment rate of 11 per cent, a $3.4 billion foreign exchange deficit, a reduction in productivity of 4 per cent last year, and a reduction in gross national product in the year 1977 of 2Vi per cent. This is not Canada. It is Sweden. That is one example of a country in serious trouble. If you put that foreign exchange deficit of $3.4 billion on a population basis
May 25, 1978

with Canada, it would be in the order of $10 billion. That country is in serious difficulty. If you go through the group of the 24 OECD countries, you will find similar problems.
I maintain we are in a serious global economic crisis when we see this situation reproduced in country after country. Most of these countries responded extremely well during the sixties and early seventies to very rapid growth. They instituted, as we did in this country, some very elaborate social services to meet the needs of the people.
All of a sudden, a new concept was introduced, a shortage of oil. The OPEC countries began draining off $100 billion to $150 billion a year in capital. From this point, we are all in some trouble. It is not the only reason for the trouble, but it is the point where we seriously began to get into trouble.
There are three major factors globally that we have to look at in terms of these problems. Quantumly in the kinds of problems that all countries are facing, there is a minimum universal rate of inflation of 5 per cent and rapidly growing unemployment, such as in Sweden. A whole series of social problems have grown in a quantum way over the past four or five years. That is the first situation.
The second is the unique situation where, perhaps for the first time in the history of mankind, we see universal shortages of energy. We all grew up with the notion that there was plenty and all we had to do was arrange our lives to take advantage of it. As I mentioned earlier, global shortages have had an effect in terms of the large drain on our dollar. Eventually, we will be required to change our lifestyle.
The third factor which is extremely important is the techniques with which we have traditionally solved these kinds of problems. The Keynesian fiscal and monetary techniques do not work any more. They do not work because of the magnitude of the problems. The problems are far too large to be solved in terms of techniques such as creating demand by sales tax and so on. One cannot reduce one million unemployed just by these techniques.
The second reason they do not work is that they are sometimes counter-productive. We are dealing with stagflation, where you have high unemployment and high inflation at the same time. These are unheard of in any conventional economic theory, at least over a long period of time globally. For these reasons these techniques are not working.
It appears we will not be embarking on an election for some months, possibly a year. It is important that we in this House and we in this nation begin to look very seriously at these long-term problems that face us. I suggest that the government embark on a series of major white papers dealing with some of the alternatives in terms of unemployment, government spending, foreign exchange problems, and energy.
I wish to outline some thoughts on the problems of unemployment. White papers should be set up so that the Canadian public will talk now and at the time of the next election about the real issues facing us. I could perhaps state some ideas on areas such as energy, but the example I wish to deal with is
Income Tax Act
unemployment, one problem that has bedevilled us more than any other single problem in the history of this country.
Canadians seem to be concerned about the notion of creating jobs. The thesis I would like to present is that we cannot possibly begin to solve our unemployment problems and substantially reduce the one million unemployed with the techniques used at the present time. We cannot solve this problem by the use of any kind of notions surrounding job creation. We cannot create enough jobs to do this.
I believe discussion about job creation has led to a myth which has made it impossible to come to grips with unemployment in this country at its present level. I want to explain this contention and give some background material which will show how this figure of one million unemployed came about.
Between 1955 and 1971 the school population of this country rose from 2.7 million to nearly 6.4 million. In other words, it increased by about 2 xh times. In the same period the over-all population increased by only one third. Putting these things together we see that the school population rose seven times as fast as the general population. This created a whole series of problems. For example, we now have more vacant classrooms in this country than we know what to do with. We had to build these schools because of the demographic bulge. I suspect there will be a reverse housing problem in a few years because fewer family units will be formed. Remember, there is a factor here of seven. The situation is beginning to change now, but it will be four or five years before the change is substantial enough to be reflected in the unemployment figures.
It is interesting to note, also, that in 1953 19 per cent of the population of Canada, from infants to people 100 years old, were in the work force, and that by 1971 this percentage had grown to 29. So there are these two factors to consider-the striking increase in the school population during the period I have referred to, and the hardly less remarkable increase in the number of the population engaged in employment. Together this had led to an almost impossible situation in terms of job creation.
The number of people working between 1970 and 1975 increased by 18.2 per cent, or 1.4 million. Look at what the OECD countries have accomplished in this field. You will see that Canada leads the group. We have created almost twice as many jobs as any country in that group. The United States has moved along, but before 1975 its record was well below ours. We have created more jobs than any nation in the industrial world. But there are still one million people unemployed. It is perfectly understandable, given the demographic situation to which I have referred.
Consider the conventional techniques one might use to solve this problem. Look at the latest review from the Economic Council. It says that if we were to achieve a 5 per cent growth rate the unemployment rate would level off at about 8 per cent in the next couple of years, and that if we raised it to 6 per cent unemployment would drop to 7.7 per cent. In other words, an increase of a full point in the g.n.p. would result in only a .3

per cent decrease in unemployment. But how do we achieve even a 5 per cent increase in the g.n.p. when the United States in the first quarter of this year had a negative growth rate- not 5 per cent, or 2 per cent, or 1 per cent, but less than zero? How do we achieve this growth when we are dealing with countries like Sweden, for example, which last year experienced a "growth rate" of minus 2.5 per cent? There are no countries in the OECD at this time which can expect more than 5 per cent.
I should like to refer to a couple statements by different economists, one known as a progressive, and the other an economist for an investment firm. They were made, of all places, on the Barbara Frumm show. The first is from David Wolfe, professor of political science at York University. He was asked whether there were any other things government could still do to improve the situation, and his answer was:
Possibly, but it would involve a more radical degree of government intervention in the economy than the government has appeared willing to undertake to date or the Canadian public at large has appeared interested in seeing the government take.
The other was from Dr. John Grant, chief economist at Wood, Gundy. But he was talking about the baby boom and the other problem I have mentioned in terms of demography, and he said:
For this Five-year period ahead its almost a superhuman effort for the economy to absorb individuals into the labour force as fast as we would like them to be absorbed
He went on to say:
I can't conceive of a policy that could bring us down to 6 per cent unemployment in, say, the next couple of years. I just don't think there is a mix we could live with that would do that.
I hope I have demonstrated that a substantial reduction of the present number of unemployed is just not possible given the techniques which are being suggested. It is not possible of solution in terms, for instance, of the Tory suggestion that we might throw another couple of billion dollars into the pot by way of providing income tax cuts. First, that amount is too small-it represents less than one per cent of the g.n.p. Second, we already have an Sll billion deficit. The New Democratic Party talks about $3.5 billion, but we still face the same problem. It is not going to work.
Hon. members opposite talk about an industrial strategy. Well, that might have some effect, but it would take five or six years for results to show, by which time the demographic situation will have changed and the unemployment rate will begin to go down on its own. I might mention that Sweden has embarked on an industrial strategy of the kind suggested and got itself into grave difficults as a result. In short, I do not believe the techniques suggested, including the present budget in terms of a massive effect, will have any basic impact.
When we talk at this point about putting the unemployed to work, one million of them, we are creating a myth which makes it impossible to approach the problem realistically. We say "Let's create more jobs", and then we do not have to think the unthinkable because we keep saying that. I think that is the problem we are facing.

I do not begin to presume to say that there are simple answers, but I think there is one thing we can look at as an alternative to job creation. We really have not looked seriously at this as yet. When we cannot create enough jobs, perhaps we should look at redistributing the work that is being done among the people who are available to do it. That may sound like a very fanciful idea. It may sound foolish, but how else can we involve the one million people who are unemployed in the labour force? Let us just look for a moment at this possibility in terms of what it really means.
There are one million people who are unemployed. The rate is 8.5 per cent. Because of the way we live and because of the customs we have developed let us accept that perhaps a 4.5 per cent unemployment rate might very well be close to zero. In other words, if we had enough jobs for everybody to work at, there still might be 4 per cent to 4.5 per cent of the population at any given time not working as a result of job turnarounds, etc. There are all kinds of reasons for this.
What I think we are looking at is reducing that one million to 500,000. In terms of man-days, a very rough calculation shows that if in every 20 days, 19 days are worked at the same hourly rate and that other day is given over to someone else, we would eliminate 500,000 people from the unemployment rolls. That sounds fanciful, and obviously that is not the way we do things, but I think there are many things we can examine. We can consider earlier retirements, educational leaves, sabbatical leaves, shorter weeks, and a very interesting thing called pairing.
As a high school principal I found, especially in the early seventies, that growth in the school population began to dwindle, and we did not need quite as many teachers. There were many people who felt they would like in some way or other to work a shorter week, or possibly to work half days and pair their jobs with others. There are all kinds of ways that can happen. For those people who worry about productivity, the studies which have been carried out indicate that each of the individuals in a pair produces more than 50 per cent of the work, more than was produced before, so we get more than 100 per cent of the work being done. In these circumstances productivity tends to grow. Some people call this work sharing. I prefer to use the phrase "redistributing work" because it at least implies that the work is still being done.
I would not be talking about redistributing work if I thought there was any other way, but I believe that the idea that we can create anywhere near the number of jobs that would be necessary to reduce the number of unemployed by half a million is just not plausible, and therefore we have to look at the other alternative, which is redistributing work. I use that as an example of the kinds of things we should be talking about and of the kinds of things which should be found in a white paper on employment, inflation or energy. These are some challenging ideas about which we have to start talking.
We have spent too much time in this House talking about the RCMP, alleged barn burnings, and this, that, and the other thing. We never seem to focus on the real world out
May 25, 1978

there, the world of real economic crisis. I hope that before we go before the public, possibly next spring, we will have looked at all these things seriously and given Canadians a chance to have dialogue. We need to have dialogue with Canadians on these problems. When we face the public, I hope we will be talking about the real problems of a world in crisis in a meaningful way.

Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to take full advantage of the time allotted to me to make some comments on Bill C-56. We know that since the beginning of this week, part of this legislation has been the main topic in the House and I would like to say first that I object to the contents of the legislation, and this is not the first time that such a thing has occurred, because it includes a number of economic and financial provisions. And of course the bill covers the proposal made by the Minister of Finance to the provinces in connection with the sales tax.
We on this side of the House realize that there are good provisions which should be supported and indeed we would be prepared to do so. Unfortunately it is impossible for us to accept some of them because we find in the bill a provision which we consider unacceptable, encroaching as it does upon provincial jurisdictions. Under the circumstances, I think we must first of all oppose this legislation fiercely as a consequence of the fact that we refuse to accept a specific measure on the sales tax; if the government had wanted to show some honesty, we could have gone on quickly to measures that would be quite welcome throughout Canada, while withdrawing this one until such time as a solution could be found to the dilemma in which the province of Quebec and the federal government find themselves with regard to the sales tax.
It is not the first time, Mr. Speaker, that we have this kind of legislation hidden inside a bill that can hardly be justified but which it is hoped the official opposition will overlook because most of the other provisions can be supported quickly. Perhaps this one should not be discussed. But I feel that part on the sales tax, which is the important part, cannot be glossed over as easily as some might have wished. Last week, I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) when he introduced this bill; naturally, he appealed to all Canadians; he made an effort to play the part of the great Canadian appealing to us to support this measure. Yesterday, I also heard some of the remarks of the Minister of Finance, as well as those of a minister representing Ontario, who blamed the province of Quebec for trying to protect its own industries. I do not understand that coming from Ontario, he does not know that industries protected under the Quebec proposal are from Ontario in a proportion of 50 per cent. In the four areas, the people in Ontario will benefit from the Quebec proposal which, and I repeat it again and again, was unanimously agreed upon by all opposition parties in the National Assembly.

In my opinion, it is an attempt to manipulate public opinion to say that the province of Quebec wants to balkanize a segment of the Canadian economy, when the federal Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has made it clear that the sectors protected by the Quebec government also exist in the neighbouring province of Ontario in a 50 per cent ratio out of 90 per cent, with the 10 per cent remaining divided among three other provinces. So, I am sorry that they should spread the idea that this measure-and the Prime Minister went even further, saying that it tends to undermine federalism, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) did not hesitate to endorse his leader's position on this matter. Besides, I put a question along those lives to the Prime Minister: Does he still believe, in view of the support which the Quebec government obtained from the Liberals in the Quebec National Assembly, from Mr. Biron's Union Nationale members, from Fabien Roy, from Mr. Samson and from others, including some I shall mention later on, that all these people seek directly and unequivocally to undermine federalism. I must say that the Prime Minister was not as brave as he was with the media. He did not give the same reply and, as a matter of fact, he did not answer my question.
We fully realized also that the Minister of Finance was pursuing a very specific goal, that of stimulating industry and, consequently, the purchasing power. I feel therefore that Quebec's proposal meets in a selective way the need to stimulate industry, taking into account, of course, Quebec's priorities; perhaps I should remind hon. members of the particular problem facing the province of Quebec: an excessive unemployment rate which gives rise to a difficult situation. And the Minister of Finance, with this proposal and in view of the sudden generosity of the federal government, wanted to satisfy the needs of Quebec with a measure which does not purport to balkanize the national economy, and this was ascertained by the federal Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I therefore do not think that the Quebec government can be blamed for wanting to help those sectors most in need. Some economic meetings in Quebec have also shown that all groups agree that these sectors should receive more help.
The Minister of Finance will say that he has tried to help the textile, footwear and clothing sectors by imposing certain barriers or certain quotas, but he waited until their situation had completely deteriorated. So the Quebec government only profits from the federal proposal. Now I wonder just how much candidness the minister has exhibited. He talks of consultations with the finance ministers, and we know perfectly well that this consultation was not as flexible as he claims. That much we know. He says over and over again that for three weeks he showed a flexibility such as no other finance minister had ever shown, and we know perfectly well that a decision had to be made at some point. The Minister of Finance also knew that nine provinces had presented their budget and that, as in the case of the Maritimes, when he

offered to pay 3 per cent of a tax under provincial jurisdiction the province would have been foolish to refuse.
In other provinces, his proposal had strings attached and that is where we see interference in provincial jurisdiction. We are told that is a question of federal and provincial powers which we talked about a moment ago. But the minister also knew that the province of Quebec had not handed down its budget and it was normal that his counterpart, whoever he might be, should want to learn first of the federal generosity to use it for the most pressing needs of his province. That was exactly the reaction of the Quebec finance minister who received, I repeat, unanimous support in the National Assembly. And how many other groups support the Quebec government proposal? It seems, Mr. Speaker, that all those people are not intelligent when the Minister of Finance continues to pretend that the Quebec proposal is unacceptable and means the division of our country.
So I think that the Minister of Finance has lost his credibility in the eyes of Quebeckers and even of all Canadians. Obviously when I ask the Prime Minister if in the circumstances he intends, to deal personally with the situation as a head of state and to reopen the negotiations and initiate a meeting with his Quebec counterpart, I think it is important for the Prime Minister of our country to understand the urgency of that issue. What are the real reasons for such stubbornness on the part of the Minister of Finance? I think that with the support coming from everywhere it is obvious that the minister has some reasons he does not want to reveal in the House. That stubbornness on the part of the Minister of Finance reflects to a certain extent the hatred of the government for the legitimately elected government of the province of Quebec, that is supported by all the opposition in Quebec and it is worrying to see that kind of reaction in the province. I understand that the Prime Minister of Canada now supports the unjustified obstinacy of the Minister of Finance. We must recall for instance their deep deception after the election of that government in the fall of 1976.
I know that the election of the present Quebec government in the fall of 1976 was the proof of the monumental failure of this government which bragged about being able to get all Canadians together to reach the objective of the Prime Minister of Canada which was national unity, but everything turned into a monumental failure in the fall of 1976. And I shall never believe that the majority of those members from Quebec will continue to support this odious obstinacy concerning the legitimate demand from the province of Quebec which is not aimed at federalism or economic balkanization in those sectors but only at meeting an urgent need for the people of Quebec.
This is why I insist, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister take the issue into his own hands. There is no doubt that the Minister of Finance has made a blunder. I have no hesitation in saying that, because of his comments concerning the Quebec government, he can no longer reestablish normal

negotiations. I believe that as a responsible leader, the Prime Minister should take matters into his own hands and initiate a meeting with the Quebec premier to find a solution to this problem in the interests of both governments.
Of course, the Prime Minister repeated at a press conference no more than 24 or 48 hours ago: If Quebec wants to negotiate something, I am willing to do so. This is going too far, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister is perfectly aware of the concern and the embarrassment that this is causing to many Canadians. However, but for a few exceptions, my colleagues from Quebec remain silent. In fact, these few exceptions will perhaps convince the Minister of Finance to change his attitude because apart from the opposition parties in Quebec, important groups are asking for a change of attitude on the part of the federal government, like the QFL did yesterday. The business executive centre has also condemned the attitude of the federal government in this affair. Moreover, there seem to be some feelings of revolt within the government party, which should normally make the Minister of Finance understand that he could lose everything on this issue. In addition, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister of Canada replied with an incredible lack of concern at a press conference that he has other things to do besides dealing with this matter.
It is both disquieting and saddening for Canadians that the Prime Minister acts in such a way on such an important issue. The Prime Minister shrinks from assuming responsibility for the issue for fear of disavowing the Minister of Finance, but he is already disavowed in the minds of Quebeckers and Canadians. The Minister of Finance lacked both competence and know how in these negotiations, as is evidenced by his stubbornness, his negative approach, the pressure he is using because they have the power and the majority to force us into accepting such a proposition on a basic principle, when we believe that any province must have the freedom to negotiate with the federal government and accept such a proposition. Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I can only point to the sell-out by members from Quebec who did not take a stand as they had a duty to do. Regretfully I must indicate this is a conspiracy against one province because it is a well known fact that all opposition parties in the Quebec National Assembly supported their government, and therefore this is turning down the whole of the Quebec people. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner), a federal minister, is bringing the proof that protected industries are shared by Ontario and three other provinces, and therefore the reasons given by the Minister of Finance are groundless. Such being the case, certainly I will not hesitate to oppose with all due vigour the Minister of Finance, who suggested he was prepared to put his political future in the balance on this bill. He is doing a very poor job of representing Quebec's interests, a very poor job of meeting his commitments to his own province's interests, and the position we all have a duty to take in
