this House at this point I am ready to share with any member who feels he has that duty to defend his province's interests in the face of a federal decision that is not accepted by that province.
I would like to refer later to the question of provincial and federal powers, since the hon. member who spoke before me expressed a concern for what he called a dilution of federal powers, on the assumption that nothing should be changed at a time when we have a $11.5 billion deficit and 1,500,000 unemployed. Well, this government has been there for ten years and the unilateral decisions it has been taking no matter what repercussions and implications there may be at the provincial level, and it is responsible for that 1,500,000 unemployed figure. Some efforts have been made, I have never denied it, but there were too few and they came too late in several cases.
I am fully aware that the government tried, but they failed to take the proper measures at the right time. They wake up today and tell us that because we have a $11.5 billion deficit and 1.5 million unemployed, we must give the federal government greater powers without adequate consultation with the provinces. Mr. Speaker, we shall never agree to such an attitude on the part of the federal government. We believe that in this matter the federal government has failed and infringed upon the provincial jurisdictions. That is why we shall oppose this legislation so long as the government does not withdraw this part, and I am sorry to say that we should like to support some other measures in this piece of legislation, but after the experience we had with other bills a few years ago, we shall certainly not be made to swallow this unsavoury pill contained in this bill.
The Minister of Finance was telling me this afternoon that a survey-I do not know where he found it-showed that 87 per cent of Quebeckers were in favour of his proposition. I hope he will not say that this 87 per cent was taken in the province of Quebec because, Mr. Speaker, I would then-
In a Montreal paper!

-find myself again in a difficult position, but today I would like to use my allotted time, even if I entertain some serious doubts about such a statement. I see that the Minister of Finance is in the House, so I ask him again to resume negotiations with the Quebec government.
I say to him again while he is here that it is up to the federal government, to the responsible government to make the first move, to set up a meeting with the Quebec government and find a solution. And a government which is no longer able to bow to the unanimous decision of the National Assembly is an irresponsible and incompetent government. It is impossible, Mr. Speaker, for the Minister of Finance to be the only one to be right in this matter. It is unacceptable and unbelievable. Besides, there are thousands of Canadians who think as I do. In the circumstances, they are trying to waste time, they are

But at the same time, another member who is more serious made some remarks and we are waiting to get some evidence in support of his allegations.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister did their best to accuse us of wanting to go to bed with the separatists. Yet they have manipulated, that is the word, public opinion and they chose to conceal the truth. I will not say that they lied but that they concealed the truth, namely that the political parties endorsed the provincial government position. They are not talking about that. The Minister of Finance tells me that Mr. Ryan has rejected the La Salle-Parizeau formula. First of all, this is a further example of public opinion manipulation. No one can claim that I set up that formula with Mr. Parizeau. It is unthinkable, Mr. Speaker! The Minister of Finance fails to say that Mr. Ryan feels the solution of direct payments to taxpayers that Mr. Chretien is trying to have adopted is inconsistent with the true federalist spirit, administratively costly, cumbersome and socially unfair. He likens that solution to a form of blackmail, Mr. Speaker. It is not I who say so nor a separatist. He believes that should the federal government act in this manner every time a province refused to endorse a program, it would be dangerous for it would exert undue pressures on the provinces and undermine local governments in the minds of the people.
That is a statement the new leader of the Liberal party made just recently. Mr. Biron made one also, as well as Mr. Fabien Roy, the Social Credit representatives and the New Democratic Party. The whole opposition, Mr. Speaker, rejects the attitude and the proposal of the Minister of Finance. Responsible organizations across the country, the QFL, the Quebec workers, are opposed to it. Mr. Laberge did not hesitate to ask the government to clarify that matter. But no, it seems that only the Minister of Finance is right.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, concerning this motion, I would like to report a few facts in connection with the financing by the Export Development Corporation of a cane sugar refining complex to be developed by Redpath Sugars Ltd. in the Republic of Ivory Coast. This sugar refining complex is an integrated project wholly-owned by the government of Ivory Coast which has committed itself to expanding and diversifying its agricultural production. To that end, Mr. Speaker, they set up a state corporation, Sodesucre, which is responsible for the production of sugar in Ivory Coast. Traditionally, this country has been importing sugar. Today, Mr. Speaker, it hopes to develop its own natural resources in order to supply its domestic market and get foreign exchange from export sales.
To establish that sugar complex, Sodesucre called for tenders internationally and Redpath Sugars Ltd. was awarded the contract, in spite of very stiff international competition from firms which were supported by state organizations equivalent to the Export Development Corporation. The successful bid of this Canadian firm resulted in suppliers and sub-contractors creating employment for Canadians.
This sugar complex which is a commercial undertaking was developed because the government of Ivory Coast felt that it was an answer to an economic need. The EDC supports commercially viable operations which involve exports profitable to Canada. By definition, such operations involve two willing parties: a buyer and a vendor. In other words, such operations must be profitable to both.
On the other hand, the expected operation must be financially viable. As it is a commercial and financial agency responsible for creating firm commercial relations for Canada, the EDC tries to deal with buyers who will prove successful. Indeed, the buyer who concludes a good deal will be able to meet his financial commitments and will become a regular customer for Canadian goods and services. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member just said, it is indeed up to the Speaker to decide what is relevant or not under the rules. And what I say is perfectly relevant but no member of the opposition will force me at the beginning of my speech to say in advance if I am for or against a bill. I shall first present my arguments. That is what I am doing. And then I shall decide myself, freely, if the Chair allows me to do so, to support or reject the motion of the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert). I know as well as the hon. member for Edmonton West the basic rules on which he insisted so much. The rules are the same for everyone. But I do not agree with him on facts and I contend that what I say is particularly relevant to the motion under consideration and that he is entitled not to agree with me. He is entitled to object if he believes that what I am saying is irrelevant, but he does not have a monopoly on truth and you have decided that what I am saying is relevant, Mr. Speaker. Later on in my speech 1 will say whether or not I support the motion. Therefore, with your permission, I shall continue to explain my position. I was saying that the operation considered must be financially sound.
Since it is a business and financial organization responsible for establishing solid business relationships on behalf of Canada, the EDC wants to do business with buyers who will make money. This is what I said a while ago, Mr. Speaker. The sale in question was announced on August 11, 1976, partly as follows: The Export Development Corporation in Ottawa will be the leader of an international pool of financial institutions which will include the Royal Bank of Canada and the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce. This pool will be responsible for financing the establishment of a $172 million sugar cane agro-industrial complex in the Republic of the Ivory Coast.
I would like to mention that this is only one of the many projects which have benefitted from the support of the Export Development Corporation through its loan, insurance and foreign investment guarantee programs. Outside the export sector, the role of the Export Development Corporation is perhaps misunderstood by the public, and I would like to take this opportunity to define its areas of responsibility and mention some of its achievements. I think it would also enlighten the hon. member for Edmonton West. It is a fascinating story that goes back to 1944 when a bill was passed on export credits insurance, creating a body whose head office was located in small quarters near Sparks street and was headed by one administrator, only one, assisted by a lone employee. According to its first annual report, published at the end of March 1945, that body had assets of $1 million in available and excess capital; it had also made $296.55 in operating profits. Since then, that body has grown and the present corporation has granted loans in the order of $4 billion to foreign buyers.

May 25, 1978
Export Development Corporation Through its programs alone, just in 1977, its support to Canadian exports exceeded $2.6 billion, Mr. Speaker.
But let us come back to the announcement made in August 1976 on the occasion of the signing by the Export Development Corporation of a loan agreement for $88.3 million for that sugar cane complex. When the Minister of Trade, Industry and Commerce (Mr. Horner) made the announcement, it was with some pride because far more was involved than just a matter of lending money to lubricate the wheels of our trade.
I would like to say a few words about the responsibilities of the corporation, Mr. Speaker. First of all, it issues export credit insurances and as such, it protects exporters against any risk of loss under circumstances beyond their control when carrying out their operations. Those risks include wars, funds freezing, removal of export or import licences and other political hazards. Included are also refusal or failure of payment by the buyer, insolvency, evasions and other commercial risks. The Canadian Export Corporation is the only agency which can provide that range of protection. It can also insure a bank or a third party against insurable risks under an export transaction. As far as insurances and guarantees are concerned, businessmen should also be able to obtain a bank credit to cover their export operations, which would not be charged against their regular line of credit. The CEC covers prior and subsequent risks to delivery either for contracts or for the delivery itself. On the whole, it covers all sales with a one year credit (short term) or a five year credit (middle term). At the end of the year the value of insured exports amounted to something like $1.3 billion.
The Corporation also grants loans to foreign buyers to help them finance the purchase of capital goods, goods and services which, according to standards internationally agreed upon, require a longer credit period, ten years for instance. It is important to emphasize this in this debate on the motion brought forward by the honourable member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), to justify the position I shall have to take in a few moments, Mr. Speaker, in answer to your suggestion. Such loans cannot be granted by Canadian financial institutions, because either of the lenght of the credit period or the interest rates. The former depends on the level of efficiency of the project and on the existing foreign competition. The loan we grant enable the exporters who are competitive as to prices, quality and delivery periods, not to lose a market for lack of competitive credits. The EDC can also provide guarantees to banks for their export loans. It also encourages banks, involvement as in these loans as much as possible and quite often Mr. Speaker without the benefit of a guarantee. The EDC is not trying to compete with the banks. It only deals with financing arrangements to help the banks. Finally the corporation insures Canadian investors against loss of their foreign investments in case of wars, riots and insurrections, confiscations or uncompensated expropriations and restrictions to the repatriation of gains or goods. This factor is uncreasingly important

for our trade and the new trend for countries which buy our goods is to constitute joint ventures. This simple description of the responsibilities of the EDC will certainly give you an idea of the complexity of the problems which we are facing at this time when our trade is becoming more and more specialized. As a matter of fact the EDC has recently launched a new program of completion guarantee for projects abroad and special aid to expanding export firms.
The Ivory Coast operation, Mr. Speaker, is somewhat exceptional in view of the fact that it is the first of the kind in Canada, as has been announced. Incidentally, Redpath Sugar Limited of Montreal has been able to hire a bilingual team of designers and engineers in Montreal. This is the first Canadian project for which three major EDC programs were used to carry out the trade objectives of our country.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, I would like to state the position I shall be taking on the motion by the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), but I see that my speaking time has nearly expired and I will have several other matters to discuss before I let this position be known. I wish to give some of my colleagues the opportunity to take the floor. To conclude I would like to mention that some other programs to which I have referred require the involvement of very important participants. The buyer, the exporter, the bank and the investor are all seeking to pursue their own interest which does not concern anyone else. The details of the projects considered cannot be made public, for it is because of the information of a confidential nature that the EDC had obtained that it could arrange the financial aspect of these projects. These details could not be released without violating the trust of the parties. On the other hand, the activities of the EDC would be hampered, which would be detrimental to Canada's trade.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make but two brief points about the motion that is before us today. In supporting the hon. member who wishes to have these papers produced, I would like to read to you once again the motion that is before us:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all correspondence, notes, minutes of meetings, documents and agreements relating to the financing by the Export Development Corporation of a cane sugar complex in the Republic of the Ivory Coast to be built by Redpath Sugars Ltd.
My first point is, as I say, that I support the motion to produce these papers. It is important to know what the arrangements are, and we should have openness in government and in financial transactions that involve the people's money. The other point of major concern in a case like this is that we have an Export Development Corporation helping a large sugar firm, the Redpath company, to establish a sugar complex in the Ivory Coast. I have a number of questions I would like to have answered with regard to that area.
May 25, 1978

I have seen now for too long large multinational corporations from the west going into the third world countries or developing countries and setting up huge complexes on the best land that is available for luxury crops, primarily goods like sugar, bananas and tobacco-crops that are not part of the necessities of life. These corporations set up on the best land and leave the secondary land for the people of those countries, in this case the Ivory Coast. It is that secondary land that these people must use to feed themselves.
Despite the fact that we have developments like this in many countries of the Third World, there is now more starvation and hunger in many of these countries than there has ever been before. The reason for this is that foreign owners like Redpath are going in and taking the best land and taking advantage of the very cheap labour that is available. Because of this the corporations are making a lot of money but they do not reinvest it in those countries. It is not a good thing to promote, nor is it a good thing for the EDC to be promoting.
It is the taxpayers' money that is financing a project of this sort, and yet, as I said earlier, the people of the Third World countries must live on secondary land and produce their food on land of inferior quality because a foreigner is using their best land to produce a luxury export. This is not a good precedent, nor do I like the importation into the Third World of this sort of agriculture, which is a psychology that North Americans seem to follow.
I do not want that method of farming and agriculture to be exported to countries of the third world because it may not be the best thing for them. Instead, we should help the countries of the developing world help themselves. We should make sure that the countries of Africa, Asia, and South America are self sufficient in food. Few countries can produce enough food to feed themselves. Countries like France and the United States can, of course, and even a small country like Israel is able to feed itself as a result of good planning and proper utilization of its resources. If we do not promote self sufficiency in food for other countries, we will have massive famine. Shortages of food in years to come will make the energy crisis look like a Sunday school picnic. When people are faced with starvation they turn to violence. The EDC should not be involved in transactions of this sort.
The other thing about this kind of development in the Third World is that it is not only important to huge agra-business companies but that those countries also import eating habits. An example is the exportation of skim milk powder to the third world and the promotion of the bottle feeding of children in those countries. This turned out to be a disaster because those children cannot digest the lactose, yet it was promoted for commercial profit. I do not want Canada, through the EDC, to be part of that sort of thing.
I think the House should support the motion for the production of papers relating to the financing arrangements made by the EDC. Just yesterday the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) questioned the Minister of Supply and Services
Export Development Corporation (Mr. Goyer) about the government's business dealings in Iran and Saudi Arabia. They are two of the wealthiest countries in the world, and anyone who doubts that should read the article in last week's Time magazine about the billions of dollars that Saudi Arabia cannot even spend. The money is coming in faster than they can spend it, yet a Canadian Crown corporation is investing in Saudi Arabia and Iran. Today in the House the minister said that the Canadian Export Development Corporation may become involved in the transaction referred to and, if it does, I say that is a crime. If Canadian industrial development is to be stimulated through the EDC it should be done in countries that can be helped, not the wealthy ones.
The motion calls for the production of documents, notes, minutes of meetings, correspondence, and so on, between the EDC and the Republic of the Ivory Coast regarding a sugar complex to be built there by Redpath Sugars Ltd. Perhaps we should also talk about the other things the EDC does and whether it should be doing them in the third world. I say it should not. It should not be investing in countries like Iran and Saudi Arabia.
I hope the government will take note of my remarks and made policy changes which will help people in the developing countries as well as the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Young (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE RELATING TO EDC FINANCING OF SUGAR COMPLEX IN REPUBLIC OF IVORY COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was going to begin by saying for the benefit of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert)-but I notice he has left the chamber-that I will be speaking against the motion. I will elucidate on the premise I intend to put this afternoon, which is that it would be adverse to the effective functioning of the Export Development Corporation if we were to expose the papers connected with this transaction. That being the case, I suggest it would mean that such a disclosure would be adverse to Canadian export sales and the interests of all of us so far as employment of Canadians is concerned.
It seems to me that the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) has serious misconceptions about how the Export Development Corporation assists other countries and Canadians. Perhaps I can give him some of the bits and pieces of information that he said he was looking for, and at the same time explain how it functions, how it helps Canadians, assists developing countries and even some of the more developed countries of the world.
The financing by the Export Development Corporation of the cane sugar complex in the Republic of the Ivory Coast should be regarded as a commercial triumph. I suggest that it is a victory by Canadian exporters. It carries benefits to exporting suppliers and sub-suppliers all the way across Canada. The project involves development and construction of a cane sugar plantation, raw sugar factory, ancillary facilities, with a new railway spur, sidings, and access roads which will link the site to the existing systems and allow transportation of the factory output to the sea for export. The government of the buyer country is the driving force behind the project and is putting up $25 million of equity, as well as guarantees of payment.

May 25, 1978
Export Development Corporation
The sugar complex is a commercial project being built because the Ivory Coast government has decided that its economy needs and can benefit from it. I want to point out to the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville that is was largely the decision of the Ivory Coast to begin this project. The EDC supports commercially viable transactions which involve exports beneficial to Canada. By definition, such a transaction involves a willing buyer and a willing seller. In other words, it must be mutually beneficial. Furthermore, it must be a financially sound proposition. As a commercial financial institution devoted to building strong, long term trading relationships for Canada, EDC wants to be involved with buyers that will prosper. The satisfied buyer engaged in a sound transaction will be able to meet financial obligations and will also become a valuable repeat customer for Canadian goods and services.
The Ivory Coast government was certainly a willing and enthusiastic buyer. It was represented at the signing of the EDC loan agreement by the minister of finance of the country, its minister of agriculture, two ambassadors, and a number of its very senior officials. Obviously the government sees long term benefits accruing to the country from the project, otherwise it would not have embarked on such a large undertaking in the first place.
The benefits to Canada are very considerable. There is nothing wrong with that. Foreign trade is our economic lifeblood, so to speak. We rely very heavily on export trade. Exports represent over 22 per cent of our gross national product. Canada is seventh in the world of exports as a percentage of gross national product and even more strikingly is second in the world in the value of exports per capita.
The project in the Ivory Coast has been profitable for Redpath Sugar and has been good business for the Export Development Corporation. The foreign investment guarantee was for $12.5 million with respect to a 12-year management contract and for technical services. This provided a substantial premium to the Export Development Corporation. But let me emphasize that the Export Development Corporation proceeded to provide its support when it was satisfied that the government of the Ivory Coast wanted the project. It was at their invitation that the project be conducted. We assume that this project was in the interest of the Ivory Coast, that it made good economic sense for them and would have a beneficial impact on the standard of living in that country.
Let me give some of the specifics about Export Development Corporation's financing with respect to the Redpath Sugar project in the Ivory Coast. On August 11, 1976, the Export Development Corporation announced that it would lead an international syndicate of lending institutions, including the Royal Bank of Canada and Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, to finance a $172 million agro-industrial raw cane sugar complex for the Republic of the Ivory Coast. Export Development Corporation is to lend up to $88.3 million for the project.

The Export Development Corporation financing involves participation by Canadian banks totalling $21.6 million which will be co-managed by the Royal Bank of Canada and Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce. In addition, Antony Gibbs and Sons Limited is participating in the amount of up to $16.7 million.
A $45 million Eurocurrency loan will be provided by a consortium of banks to assist in the local cost financing, start-up working capital and contingencies. The loan will be co-managed by Citicorp International Bank Limited, New York, the Royal Bank of Canada, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and Brandts Limited, London.
A project of Redpath Sugars Limited, Montreal, principal subsidiary of Redpath Industries Limited, Toronto, the 14,800 acre complex in the west African French speaking nation, will provide 60,000 tons of raw sugar for export annually. The deal was the first of its kind for Canada. It was largely due to the assembly, by Redpath, of a bilingual engineering team based in Montreal that the project was a Canadian one and not American or British.
Value of Canadian goods and services to be financed under the Export Development Corporation agreement will exceed $74 million. Export Development will also provide preshipment insurance for Canadian goods and services, as well as guaranteeing the Redpath investment in the form of a longterm management and technical assistance contract. This was the first time all three operating divisions of the corporation have been jointly involved in concluding a project of such magnitude.
Redpath's contract includes responsibility for construction and management of all phases of operation from land preparation to product shipment. This involves development of a sugar plantation, an irrigation system, a molasses terminal, a sugar factory and all necessary infrastructure including a rail spur and marine terminal. The sugar factory, molasses terminal and irrigation system will be handled on a turnkey basis.
A substantial part of capital goods and services will be procured from exporting suppliers and sub-suppliers from accross Canada. The realization of this object has put Canada in a most favourable position for further export sales related to sugar production.
Redpath Industries Limited is a diversified company involved in sugar refining, construction materials manufacturing and engineering, and agricultural consulting services. It employs more than 1,700 people in Canada and abroad.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I describe the project as somewhat of a triumph. I suggest that for the proper functioning of these facilities provided by Export Development Corporation there must be an element of trust between the Export Development Corporation and its client, exporters and investors, and a similar degree of trust between Export Development Corporation and its correspondents, the banks and similar institutions at home and abroad.
The corporation is on the inside, so to speak, of business deals large and small. In each one the exporter has to trust
May 25, 1978

Export Development Corporation to safeguard information involving particulars of the exporter's business affairs. That trust would be totally destroyed if the confidentiality were broken. These confidences create an obligation. More than a mere government agency fondness for secrecy is involved. To produce papers of a commercially confidential nature would be to require a breach of that trust.
The project in question, an integrated sugar complex, is wholly owned by the government of the Ivory Coast, a government which has committed itself to expanding and diversifying its agricultural base. In an effort to do just this, it created Sodesucre, a government owned corporation to assume responsibility for the production of Ivorian sugar. The country has traditionally imported sugar, and hopes to develop its own national resources to supply the domestic market and provide the country with foreign exchange earnings from export sales.
Sodesucre called for tenders in the international market for the development of the sugar complex, and in response to this call Redpath Sugars submitted a successful bid. The bid was won in the face of stiff international competition from firms which were supported by their national equivalents to Export Development Corporation. The successful bid of the Canadian firm has resulted in the placing of substantial equipment orders in Canada and has created jobs for Canadians by these suppliers and their sub-suppliers.
The sugar complex is a commercial project being built because the ivory Coast government has decided that its economy needs and can benefit from it. The Export Development Corporation supports commercially viable transactions which involve exports beneficial to Canada. By definition, such a transaction involves a willing buyer and a willing seller. In other words, it must be mutually beneficial. Furthermore, it must be a financially sound proposition. As a commercial financial institution devoted to building strong long term trading relationships for Canada, Export Development Corporation wants to be involved with buyers that will prosper.
This project represents the first chance that a Canadian company has had to export a sugar cane complex. It was also the largest project of any kind realized by Canada in West Africa. All of this has been made possible by a unique and ingenious blend of the three facilities available through Canada's EDC. It has not been mentioned that Canada is perhaps the only country in which all three such facilities are available under one roof, available through the same government agency. The EDC is an agency, incidentally, that costs the taxpayers nothing except the share capital paid into it for the shares the government holds, and in 1977 EDC made a profit of $18.7 million or 11 per cent on the equity.
It has been mentioned that among the international syndicates which EDC is leading are Canadian banks; the Royal Bank of Canada and the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce are lending U.S. $16.6 million. It was pointed out earlier that banks are not in the business of making loans repayable over a term as long as ten years. The EDC has so
Export Development Corporation
arranged the financing that the banks' share will be on terms acceptable to the bank's normal practices. They will be repaid out of the first five repayment instalments. Thus we can say the banks' funds will be in for a portion of the construction period and a portion of the repayment period, probably not more than five years, so that the funds can be made available without going beyond the normal five or so years maximum for bank funds.
EDC disburses its loan funds and the banks also disburse their loan funds as payments become due to the exporter under the terms of the sale. For goods and services sold by Canadians the disbursements are made to the Canadian exporter or suppliers as delivery is made or performance is carried out. A small percentage may be applied to local costs of the project, under EDC's practice. The banks' funds are not normally tied to Canadian exports. Thus EDC disburses its loan funds to the Canadian supplier. The money stays here in Canada.
What happens if there is a disaster, or a breach by the borrower of a predisbursement condition? In such a case the EDC can protect the exporter by insurance, credits insurance, commonly called pre-shipment cover, which will cover those risks until the time payment is received. Thus the second of the EDC facilities has been blended into this transaction.
Sugar manufacture has gone a long way from the days of the windmill and open fired vats. Will the borrowers be able to manage a modern plant with all the technological refinements, if I may use the term, of a sugar operation? Redpath will not stay in the Ivory Coast indefinitely, and after it leaves trained personnel will be essential. Provisions have been made to cover that eventuality. Redpath and the buyer have arranged a management contract and a training contract which includes training in Canada in the French language of some 50 Ivorians. So that need has been taken care of.
The management contract brings into play the foreign investment guarantee facility of the EDC. It is an "investment in a foreign country" within the Export Development Act, the statute which has created the machinery for these guarantees. Thus if Redpath were unable to repatriate its earnings from the contract or if the government of the Ivory Coast were to repudiate the contract, the resulting loss would be covered by the foreign investment insurance policy. Thus the third of EDC's three facilities was employed in this sale.
I think it would be gratifying to the House to observe how the wise and beneficial measures parliament has provided are employed to bolster our foreign trade and encourage its development, not by subsidy, but by reasonable, sane and sensible operations carried out in a businesslike way.
Let me emphasize that the exporter, Redpath Sugars Limited of Montreal, employs about 1,700 people in Canada. It is Canada's largest producer of refined sugar. It operates two sugar cane refineries in Canada. This company is the principal subsidiary of Redpath Industries Limited of Toronto, which in turn is slightly more than 50 per cent owned by Tate & Lyle Investments Limited of London, England. The Montreal company certainly has the expertise to carry out successfully the

May 25, 1978
Export Development Corporation
interesting Ivory Coast project of which we have been speaking.
Still more importantly, perhaps, is the favourable position in which Canada will be for further export sales related to sugar production when the Ivory Coast operation comes into production. There is a real Canadian identity in this sale. Mr. Speaker, those further sales and the sale we have been speaking of mean jobs for Canadians. Reference has been made at some length to the Export Development Corporation, and in one word that is what it stands for-jobs. As we have said, to expose all the papers connected with this important transaction is adverse to the effective functioning of the EDC. In the simplest terms that means adverse to Canadian export sales and against the interests of all of us so far as employment in Canada is concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: CORRESPONDENCE RELATING TO EDC FINANCING OF SUGAR COMPLEX IN REPUBLIC OF IVORY COAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this private member's motion was introduced I had, frankly, no reason to get involved in the discussion; but as I sat here this afternoon I found myself irritated by exactly the same kind of nonsense we have heard for years-what is good for the EDC is good for the country. Or, in other words, what is good for General Bullmoose is good for the country.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Young) tells us EDC costs the country nothing. That may be so. But how is it, then, that in the last few minutes in another room closure was almost forced on a committee because the government wanted to raise the appropriation for EDC from $8 billion to $20 billion? If EDC costs us nothing, why should the government be using all its weight to put another $12 billion into the institution? I have great difficulty imagining $18,000 let alone $18 million or $18 million. Yet all of sudden this corporation which costs us nothing is to get $ 12 billion more.
I rise this afternoon to say thank you to the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) who has the courage of his convictions, though his colleagues and the government obviously oppose him, in asking for the production of papers to show what happens when the EDC sponsors a Canadian firm operating in a foreign country. One thing the hon. member for Niagara Falls did was to lay before us a lot of figures, millions of dollars for this, hundreds of thousands of dollars for that. Obviously, somebody knows the answers to all these questions. If the hon. member can submit this information so readily, why should it be so difficult to get a look at some of these papers?
Questions were asked in the House this afternoon. For instance, the ministers were asked to explain why the government, through EDC, was investing in countries like Iran and Saudi Arabia, to the tune of $500 million or $1 billion. My understanding of the current world situation is that those countries have enough money of their own. But the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) stood up and accused us of threatening to take away jobs from Canadian farmers and workers if we as much as raised a whisper against the EDC. I do not buy that balderdash, frankly. 1 believe that given the right climate Canadian firms would export a great deal more than they are now. But I do not believe this aura of

secrecy is needed. Nor do we need the heavy hand of government, the inference that when we ask questions on this subject we are threatening Canadian unity or employment possibilities or doing all kinds of nasty things.
What does the government have to hide? What is there in a contract that is so very secret? If a major Canadian company dealt with a contract overseas, at its annual shareholders' meeting it would certainly be forced to reveal some of the details of that contract. Private enterprise has to do it. Why is it so difficult for the government to bring some of these papers before us? What is there in this government that it is so bound up in secrecy?
I might just digress momentarily. I intend to bring this up before this session is closed. All of us know that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) caused quite a flurry in the House just recently when there was a question regarding someone looking at his income tax files. That has been exaggerated to the most ridiculous extent.
I tried the other day, in order to help an aged veteran, to get the date of his discharge from the Canadian forces. I was told that that was a secret and that I had to get a letter from that veteran authorizing me to ask the question. That is utter nonsense. All of us know that one of the things we do most frequently is intercede on behalf of our constituents in matters arising out of conflicts with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Now we are being told that in the future when we ask questions of the Unemployment Insurance Commission we will have to have letters from our constituents authorizing us to ask those questions. This is happening now with regard to income tax. What is there about this government that it wants to hide everything? I heard as a joke some time ago that the government wanted to keep secret the number of cans of dog food on the DEW line. I sincerely believe that the government would hide almost anything.
I want to hear this government tell us why it is going to hide all these documents, but before I sit down I want to say that I admire the hon. member for Vaudreuil for bringing this matter forward and asking very simply that these papers be produced. I must ask again, why is the government trying to hide them?

Every time the Corporation wants to increase its authorized capital stock in order to help our Canadian firms export, sell

goods and thereby create jobs, it must indeed come before Parliament.
It is clear that the Opposition is asking why the EDC needs so much leeway to manoeuvre. No later than this afternoon in committee I had to explain once again to the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) that if the Corporation-

There is secrecy, that principle of confidentiality which might affect the competitive position of the company by divulging some technical aspects, some aspects of their knowhow. There is a very simple reason for that; you may borrow $100,000 at 8 per cent but all the other terms of the contract may affect the terms and the cost of borrowing.
However, Mr. Speaker, Redpath Sugar Ltd. is another case where the Export Development Corporation was involved to create employment in Canada. If I may refer to the New

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Chretien that Bill C-56, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to authorize payments related to provincial sales tax reductions, be read for the second time and referred to the committee of the whole, and of the amendment (Mr. Broadbent) (p. 5548).

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying before the five o'clock recess, in my capacity as representative of a province which has its own problems, I am quite sorry to see that few members from that province have disagreed with the Minister of Finance who rejected the Quebec proposal which, I repeat, would not jeopardize the incentives or objectives advocated by the Minister of Finance, namely a stimulus to the economy and to the industry and more purchasing power. And I think that my friends from the province of Quebec know perfectly well that the Quebec proposal is the right response to those two basic requirements and will provide an incentive to crucial sectors of the Quebec industry, and is supported, as I said earlier, by Ontario and three other provinces. The sales tax reduction will amount not to 3 per cent but to 8 per cent and I challenge my friends opposite to pretend that this is not a solution or proposal acceptable for the province of Quebec and honourable for the rest of Canada.

May 25, 1978
Income Tax Act
When I look back, Mr. Speaker, on what took place over the last few weeks, and am confronted with this arrogance, this stubbornness, I will not hesitate in accusing the federal government of dishonesty. And what about its prejudiced attitude towards the Quebec move to abolish the sales tax in the soft sectors of its industries? I shall refer you to a recent study in support of the Quebec proposal, by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce which shows that in the four sectors where the sales tax was cut out altogether, namely clothing, textile, shoes and furniture, about 122,000 workers out of 270,000 are working in Canada outside the province of Quebec, which clearly proves that the Minister of Finance's allegation that this measure is aiming at the balkanization of the Quebec economy is groundless and deceitful. In fact, it is only in the clothing industry that Quebec has more workers, that is one third of a total number of 121,000 in Canada. I say that by voluntarily suppressing those figures and having us believe that the Quebec proposal is prejudicial to the national interests, the government is misleading the people and is resorting to some kind of political deception which is unworthy of a government with the least sense of honour, Mr. Speaker. A good number of manufacturers in the industries involved outside Quebec have recognized that the other provinces would profit by the withdrawal of the sales tax and not only Quebec, as the government and the Minister of Finance would have us believe.
Once again, Ottawa has infringed upon a field coming under provincial jurisdiction, and because Quebec stands up for its economic priorities and to protect the interests of its citizens, it is taxed with being separatist and with trying to balkanize the Canadian economy. This is just not so, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister and his assistants know it quite well, even though they are suffering from chronic federalitis to the extent that they are unable to admit that Quebec can be right without jeopardizing Canadian unity.
The economists, industrialists and political commentators of Canada, even Anglophone, are virtually unanimous in agreeing that the Quebec counter-proposal is likely to stimulate employment, an objective pursued by the Minister of Finance, while at the same time increasing by 8 per cent the purchasing power of Quebec residents. That can only help the national economy and constitute an element of economic revival. Though the complete abolition of the sales tax as advocated by Quebec seems to have favourable effects on the economy throughout the land, the gentlemen heading this government maintain that it is a subversive manoeuvre. According to their reasoning, the formula cannot be beneficial since it supposes a special arrangement with a provincial government. Still, during the negotiations prior to the minister's budget, he himself managed to accommodate the special requests of British Columbia, which delights us, of Saskatchewan, Ontario and the Maritimes. But when it comes to Quebec, that is
[Mr. La Salle.)
asking too much, and as they see it it threatens to split the country asunder.
I say most emphatically that if our party were in power now, we would not hesitate in handing over to Quebec, on their own conditions, that is for the pursuit of two objectives, the full amount of $226 million, to which they are entitled under the formula initially proposed by the minister himself. There would be no hesitation either in giving the same advantages, of course, and the same consideration to the provinces which would voice such a wish.
At this point in my comments, Mr. Speaker, I say that the government's present attitude is close to being ridiculous, and that it amounts to mere stubbornness in these circumstances. I conclude by saying that I charge this government with deliberately seeking a pretext to wage war on the government of Quebec on the eve of an election. This will perhaps enable them not to lose face in front of certain provinces but as far as I am concerned, I call this hypocrisy, falsehood and electoral fraud.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important that Canadians in general and Quebeckers in particular, be made aware of the position taken on this matter by the hon. members who represent them. All Quebeckers, I was reading this morning in the papers, it is unbelievable, when the Minister of Finance tells me that he saw, in the Journal de Montreal, the results of a survey showing that 87 per cent of Montrealers favor his proposal. Is it possible, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance should rely on a survey conducted by a newspaper, the Journal de Montreal, which is a serious paper, but this survey may have been rigged by a group of individuals who would report that 87 per cent are supporting Mr. Chretien's proposal. I see how naive he is when he refers to this seriously, just as naive as when he submitted his proposal to a province that had not yet presented its budget.
Quebeckers must know that the Finance Minister's proposal is far from contributing to the just society promised by this champion of national unity, this champion of inflation and unemployment, this czar of the provinces who has promised to give us heaven during the last ten years. Mr. Chretien's proposal amounts to gross injustice. That is unfortunate, but I think the leader of the Liberal party was speaking about it yesterday in Quebec City when he said that he found this solution inconsistent with the true spirit of federalism. That was Mr. Ryan speaking, and Mr. Ryan, Mr. Speaker, is no separatist as far as I know. This solution is administratively costly, cumbersome and socially unfair. It is not Mr. Parizeau who said that but the leader of the Quebec Liberal party.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) says that he will compensate for the Quebec refusal by distributing $85 cheques in certain cases, $22, $42 cheques or nothing in other cases, but nearly one million workers in Quebec will not receive this cheque from the federal government. For instance, a young couple who both work and who both paid their $85 in taxes
May 25, 1978

will receive $85 each or $170. I am very happy for this young couple, Mr. Speaker, but in a family with six children, where the mother cannot have an outside job, the father who must work hard every day will only get $85. No one can tell me that this is the just society promised by the Prime Minister who has certainly not kept his promises. Quebeckers are starting to realize that the dream of 1968, the just society, paradise in Canada, has become a deep disillusion in the last few months, since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made his decision recently about the possibility of going to the country. Dr. Gallup advised him not to call an election for a while yet, but for a number of Quebeckers, I believe that this dream will determine the future position of the party in power. No one in Quebec remains untouched by this basic issue. We are defending a matter of principle. We want a viable federalism where the provinces will participate truly in major national decisions. It is only in this way that there can be co-operation in Canada, and not in the way that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are now behaving. This is stubbornness, Mr. Speaker. Because of too many deceptions, too many disagreements, too much confrontation and arrogance on the part of the federal authorities.
I remember very well that I endorsed requests from Quebec members, from the Quebec government at the time of Mr. Johnson. I was accused of supporting the Union Nationale. I supported the submissions of Mr. L'Allier, Mr. Hardy, Mr. Saint-Pierre, when the government in Ottawa turned down recommendations which were perfectly justified in view of the rather special situation of Quebec. We are accused of being bedpartners with separatists. That is hogwash, Mr. Speaker, and the Minister of Finance knows it. He is disavowed at this very moment by the whole province of Quebec and he has surely lost much credibility across the country. It is a clear fact that the Minister of Finance has made a colossal mistake.
He has not the courage to recognize his error and correct it, and he is now proving, Mr. Speaker, that federalism as suggested and described by Mr. Levesque cannot work. He is proving it with the complicity of members opposite from Quebec who refuse to understand that the situation is serious. They are proving that Mr. Levesque is right when he suggests that federalism cannot work by rejecting a proposal with which most Quebeckers agree, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, this is the House of Commons; I realize that some have a Latin temper, but once again I would ask the hon. member for Joliette to be kind enough to listen to me. If he is not satisfied, he could ask questions. Mr. Speaker, there has been consultation with the ten provinces. The Minister of Finance has received the agreement of nine of them, the other one has given no answer. It is possible, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance-oh! it is easy to play politics backwards; the hon. member for Joliette is an expert in this field-it is possible that the Minister of Finance has been imprudent. But what is his mistake? He believed that the others too would play the game of federalism. That is his mistake, Mr. Speaker, to have believed in the rules of the federalist game. Having said that, the province of Quebec reacted a few days later with its budget and made public its own sales tax reduction scheme on a selective basis applied to four sectors seen as priorities. Nobody says, Mr. Speaker, that these sectors have no priority. Nobody says, Mr. Speaker, that they should not have reduced the sales tax by 8 per cent. Nobody says, Mr. Speaker, that they were wrong to put the emphasis on the sectors they felt they had to encourage. Nobody ever said that, Mr. Speaker. To my knowledge, nobody ever said that.
Let us make a distinction! We are living in a federation. Since we are living in a federation, there are national interests,
Income Tax Act
provincial interests, and municipal interests, and you also find a federal government, a provincial government and a municipal government. The federal government, Mr. Speaker, proposed a measure designed to spur the economy throughout Canada. Nine provinces accepted, one did not answer. One province, that same one which did not answer, came up a few days later with its own formula. And then it tried to impose upon us its own conclusions because that is what it wanted to do. It wanted to play the game its own way, all by itself. It did not want to play the federal game. It wanted to play the game of the province of Quebec. What are the facts, Mr. Speaker, what are they? In the Maritimes, where the provinces do not have a very strong manufacturing structure, the Minister of Finance suggested that we would pay their sales tax, I mean the reduction, that we would compensate for the loss of revenue due to the sales tax reduction, these 3 per cent. In other provinces, different arrangements were submitted. Quebec, Ontario, Saskatchewan, Manitoba would have to pay 1 per cent, the federal government taking over the other 2 per cent.
By doing away with its 8 per cent sales tax, Quebec figured that this was perhaps not a bad idea at all, Mr. Speaker, and that it just had to squeeze the lemon and see to it that it would not cost them a cent. The problem is again that they will always try their little Parizeau deal but they stand all alone, while the federal Minister of Finance has ten provinces behind him. He is in charge of a federation, you see, Mr. Speaker. When he makes a proposal, Mr. Speaker, he is dealing with ten finance ministers and if the Ministers of Finance were all like Mr. Parizeau, I can tell you that life would be a lot harder in this country because that man wants to play the game his way all by himself. Incidentally, what are the counter-proposals made by Mr. Parizeau? What are they, I ask you? None has come up since the beginning of this debate. All he said was actually "take it or leave it". So much for negotiations, Mr. Speaker! Take it or leave it! You assume entirely the loss of revenue from the sales tax in the four priority sectors on an 8 per cent basis. This is our final position.
The Minister of Finance has played the game from a federal point of view. He made a proposal. He got no answer. Let us admit that he made a mistake. A few days later, maybe one week later, he forwarded a proposal to the Minister of Finance Parizeau. He said: Listen, you have four priority sectors. We might have discussed it before but let us suppose we have been through all that. We shall let you allocate the 1 per cent you should have normally spent for that cut on the four priority sectors you have identified and we are going to pay 2 per cent on everything else. It was perfectly logical, but then there was a problem. The problem was that Mr. Parizeau had to finance a part of his proposal. He does not want to finance it, he wants the whole pie, he wants to press the lemon dry. He wants to get the $220 million without having to pay out a single penny.

Mr. Speaker, that proposal from the Minister of Finance was something different from his original stand. You cannot call this inflexibility, Mr. Speaker. I think that even the hon. member for Joliette must admit that there has been a compromise between the original proposal and the 2 per cent "across the board" proposal. Mr. Speaker, I keep hearing the hon. member for Joliette from behind the curtains, and having made his speech earlier, he should let me speak now. Mr. Parizeau rejected his proposal. After that, a few Quebeckers realizing that the situation was heading towards a dead end, asked the federal Prime Minister whether he was willing to promise that those funds would finally be paid to the province of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister promised that the funds owed to the province of Quebec would be handed over to the province of Quebec.
What was the next step? The next step was getting bogged down, unfortunately. Now I come to the definition I gave earlier, Mr. Speaker. What was behind that budget proposal? Objectives. What are those objectives? An economic recovery to join with the upturn in the economy which should have some results next fall. The objectives were to make the link. What was the ideal? Consultation. For the first time, provincial ministers of finance were consulted about a federal budget, in order to help precisely the economy to attain its cruising speed. What was the principle? A very simple principle in a federation. It is for a central government to see to it as much as possible that resources are distributed in all parts of the federation, even if some adjustments have to be made through negotiations, adjustments which were made in the case of five provinces. What were the terms and conditions, Mr. Speaker? That is where things went wrong.
Since Mr. Parizeau refuses the offers made by the Minister of Finance, the minister must find ways to return to the Quebec economy and turn over to Quebeckers and eventually to the Quebec government the funds which cannot be distributed for lack of an agreement. Several proposals have been suggested. As a matter of fact, there have been four proposals.
First of all, there is this proposal which Mr. Parizeau would like us to accept because it would solve some of his problems, and I say some, Mr. Speaker, because it would give rise to problems of another kind, about which I shall say nothing just now. So, let us assume that the federal government turns over to the Quebec government a cheque for $226 million to Finance the 8 per cent reduction in the four priority sectors. It is a possibility, but a possibility which does not make sense under the present circumstances for a number of reasons. First, it runs counter to the principle of equality which I explained a while ago. Should a province receive a cheque for $226 million-for that matter, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) stated a while ago: Well, if we are elected, we promise to give them $226 million. And he added: But if other provinces want to do the same thing, they will get the same

amount. What kind of a low calibre policy is this that the Canadian population is expected to swallow? They should at least try to meet their objectives, because otherwise it will be a monumental flop. For the moment, it is a flop in Quebec. It is not a flop elsewhere. It is working very well in nine provinces up to this time.
Mr. Speaker, let us talk about the various possibilities. The first one is to give $226 million. It is impossible because, as I said earlier, it goes against a basic principle. It also goes against the most basic rules of negotiation. If you have negotiated something, it is more or less the same as if you have signed a collective agreement with one or two unions, and a third one comes along and says: Listen, we want such or such a thing. The first two unions will not be very happy if you give something to the third that you did not give either to the second or to the first.
If you have agreed on something, you must respect your agreement and do so for everyone. Moreover, this transfer of $226 million is not logical for another reason. I cannot see why the Minister of Finance would give a cheque of $226 million to Quebec when the other provinces will not receive immediately the sums to which they are entitled since they will get this amount in the form of fiscal rebates over a period of six months in 1978. Quebec would therefore have an unfair advantage over the other provinces over a period of six months. This is another possibility, that of fiscal rebates. These rebates can seem very attractive at first glance, but I shall come back to this later on. The third possibility is a tax credit for taxpayers. What is a tax credit? Federal taxpayers simply paid income tax to the federal government. We are making tax room for a certain amount of fiscal points. We are rebating taxpayers the monies involved, so that provincial government may tax in that field. I see nothing bad with that. I cannot understand why there is so much excitement. I do not understand the outcry. There is nothing so horrendous about that, it is simply a matter of provision. There is no principle involved. None, Mr. Speaker, it is merely a matter of provision. I do not say it is the best one, but it is a simple provision. There is no question of principle involved. And what is the principle? It is to rebate $226 million. Once the principle is accepted, we turn to the provision. And what is the available means? It is to rebate an income tax credit for the province to collect. Why is it somewhat more complicated in Quebec? In fact, it is rather more apparent in Quebec. Quebec is the only province with its own revenue department, and I am not judging that in any way. So it collects its own income tax, with its own income tax returns. You have on the one hand the Canadian government collecting its own taxes, and the province doing the same. In other provinces the Canadian government, through Revenue Canada, collects for both levels of government and pays the provinces their share. In other words, to make room for the income tax credit in the nine other provinces, because this in effect was done, the Canadian government vacated a tax field

to the tune of $100, allowing the provinces to increase their income taxes by that amount. Nothing shows on the income tax return. The Canadian government gets a cheque and then distributes the money. In Quebec, things are slightly different because they are more apparent. There is an income tax credit.
The fourth possibility that was not used but that is still available was to rebate $226 million pro-rated on the Quebec population. This way everyone would get a cheque, every Quebecker at least would get a cheque for $45. Trying to understand somewhat the confusion perpertuated by opposition members, it is more or less the formula they were putting forward two weeks ago. They have changed their views two or three times since then, but that was the Clark formula, that of allegedly reimbursing the poor.
But that does not make much sense in taxation, and it is administratively extremely complex. Thus there are two possible formulas left: the tax credit and the tax rebate. The Minister of Finance retained the tax credit. I have no objection in principle, and I repeat, Mr. Speaker, I have no objection in principle because there is no principle involved. As a matter of principle, whether they choose a tax rebate or a tax credit makes no difference at all. I repeat it a third time, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is the basic factor, it is the key which will enable us to get out of this dilemma which some newsmen take pleasure in maintaining because it serves their purpose and makes the news, I think, but never mind the newsmen for the moment. The key is that there is no principle involved. What was the principle? It was to remit $226 million to Quebec so that the government of Quebec can take over this tax field and finance its own activities. There is no invasion of the provincial field, but where is the invasion of the provincial field, Mr. Speaker? You know, so many falsehoods have been spread around. Besides, members opposite have had their share in that matter. There have been so many falsehoods, so much lack of understanding in all that matter that there comes a point when one must restate the facts. There are principles, possibilities, ideals and objectives involved. Let us make a distinction. The possibilities are as follows. A tax credit. The Minister of Finance proposes that $85 be refunded to each Quebec taxpayer, and I mean Quebec taxpayer at the federal level. We are then accused of proposing a socially unjust measure. I surely would like to know why. It is quite easy to launch accusations once again but they should be able to substantiate them.
Why is it socially unjust? Why is it that by making tax room, because this is what we are actually doing by issuing a cheque to allow the provinces or the province of Quebec to move into a tax field, we are applying a socially unjust measure? I would like someone to explain that to me because I fail to understand. Would it be more just to give $45, because I am returning the argument, would it be more just to give $45 to all Quebec taxpayers, and then the government of Quebec steps in and taxes the Quebec taxpayers-who are more or less

the same as the federal taxpayers who have actually received only $45-to the tune of $85 because they still have to finance the whole debt!
But is it more just this way? This question has not been answered yet, and I would like somebody to answer it once for all. The tax credit is $85 and not $100 as in the case of the other provinces. The reason for this is also quite simple to understand. It is because the Minister of Finance has agreed to give $40 million to the province of Quebec to finance 2 per cent of the sales tax reduction in four priority sectors. I must admit that I have no objection whatsoever to that, even if I doubt that it is in complete accordance with the original proposal, but this is another story. The Quebec government will get $40 million, and I suppose it will manage to get the rest. Anyway, logic-and I do not say that pure logic necessarily goes with pure politics-logic would have required us to take a position and to stick to it, from A to Z. For example, the tax credit should have been $100 for everybody; thus Quebec would have had to get the $226 million it needs. But these are only technicalities since on the question of principle it does not make much difference to the Quebec government to receive either $40 million from the federal government and $186 million from the taxpayers or $226 million from the taxpayers, even though in practice it makes a slight difference.
However, there was another possibility, that is a tax rebate. It has certain advantages and disadvantages. First of all, it has the advantage of avoiding the obvious administrative problems involved in the $85 refund because to do this, you must take the tax tables for 1978, or what is left of them, and make the deduction at source for an x amount, for instance, 10 tax points in the case of Quebec-I believe it would be 10 in this case-and you must tell the province of Quebec: You will increase your own tax tables for the equivalent amount. What happens then? This implies fairly large expenses for businesses and administrative problems in preparing the tables, but those again are problems that can always be solved in cooperation with the Quebec department of revenue.
So, for 1978, what you would do would be simply to give a tax rebate for a certain number of tax points so that Quebec could, and again this is the same principle, tax within its temporary tax points for a period of six or three months-if the period was six months, it would be ten points, if the period was three months, it would be 20 points. I suppose that there would be problems with the tax tables, but here again, I believe it is possible to come to some agreement with the Quebec department of revenue.
This is a possibility, this is the system that Mr. Ryan supports. There is nothing to get excited about. Why should there be? Why the other system, but not this one? In any event, those are possibilities and possibilities can always be discussed. There is something else that I could perhaps urge the Minister of Finance to try, because we cannot be certain that the other side would agree to this suggestion, and this

Mr. Speaker, there is a moral to be drawn of all this. Sometimes, the best intentions give rise to problems in politics. Sometimes, logic and feelings are incompatible for all sorts of reasons beyond anyone's control. Sometimes, the population or the politicians of different levels of government fail to understand each other because they do not speak the same language. Sometimes, it is next to impossible to put forward logical, reasonable, realistic arguments. Yet, that is what I tried to do tonight, Mr. Speaker. And 1 can assure you it is not easy, because even if the hon. member for Joliette might call us traitors, it is quite easy to call someone names. Mr. Speaker, I have always thought that logic was worth a fight at least once. An attempt had to be made to quietly solve these problems which are not really so complicated, Mr. Speaker, to suppress emotions for 40 minutes and try to prove that the objectives were worthwhile, that the ideal was lofty, and that the whole thing fizzled out because of technicalities, a speck of dust having lodged in the wheel axle. In short, Mr. Speaker, I would be the last one to put the blame on the Minister of Finance, because I say once again that he has done a terrific job and has broken new ground. He was the first to discuss tax matters with the provinces while preparing his budget, and that, Mr. Speaker, nobody will be able to take it away from him.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us deals with tax measures which the present government, under the direction of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), bungled in an unprecedented way. I say that because never in our history has a government attempted to hand out money to Canadians only to find themselves under near unanimous attack by all, including their Liberal colleagues in Quebec and elsewhere, and, I may add, here within their own caucus as well.
I will not dwell on this subject of underwriting provincial sales taxes because many of my colleagues before me have dealt with that subject in detail, and more have yet to make numerous worthwhile comments on the matter in the days and perhaps weeks ahead. I would like instead to deal with some of the small business measures that were announced this week by the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) and others.
In introducing these long-awaited announcements on small business, the government created a three-ring circus equivalent to a tragi-comedy drama. Not only did the government choose to spread the announcements on one subject matter over a three-day period, but they did it in such a manner that they once again demonstrated a shameful disregard for parliament by ignoring parliamentary traditions.

On Tuesday, the "minister irresponsible for small business" bypassed the House of Commons by allowing himself to be led by the nose to the weekly news conference of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) where he read his statement to the most unimpressed media we have ever seen. I was not there, but someone said there were only two questions for the minister. One was, why was he there; and, second, when was he leaving? I am not sure whether that was a fact, but someone suggested that was the case. By announcing what he thought to be new measures outside the House of Commons, he shamefully ignored parliament.
By the reception he received at that press conference, he was moved the next day to table in the House of Commons his second phase of his announcement which dealt with a study on improving the equity financing environment for small business in Canada. A very important topic indeed, and yet the minister again ignored parliamentary procedures, this time by declining to make a statement on motions, thereby removing the rights of all members of parliament to question the minister on this very important subject.
The third part of the three-ring circus came today when the Minister of Finance tabled tax measures related to small business, again without giving the traditional statement. It is obvious that this "charade" was meant to receive maximum exposure for the government and the Minister of State in view of their lack of public activity within the small business sector, particularly when compared to what our party has been proposing in this regard in the last months and years.
I am not one for quoting newspapers, Mr. Speaker. However, Don McGillivray put it correctly when he wrote in his column published in the Montreal Gazette, Wednesday, May 24, and I quote:
We are not having the election. But we are having the campaign, which has now turned into a campaign for victory in the Gallup poll as a prelude to victory in the eventual election.
So the small business plank from the Liberal campaign platform was produced at a Trudeau press conference. The press gallery reporters, gathered for their weekly joust with the Prime Minister, found themselves confronted as well by Tony Abbott, the apple-cheeked Minister of State for Small Business.

He went on to write, and I quote:
What Abbott had to say was mostly fluff... Canadians have learned in the past to treat election promises with some reserve. But we are now in a new
May 25, 1978

situation in which a government that has called no election is likely to conduct its day-to-day administration as though it were part of a political campaign.
The episode also suggested that Trudeau and his colleagues will bear watching as they try to run a government and a campaign at the same time.
That, Mr. Speaker, basically indicates the fiasco surrounding the various announcements this week, and what makes it more serious is the fact that we in the official opposition, as well as a vast number of small business concerns across Canada, have been pressing the government for years to introduce and implement realistic incentive-oriented programs helpful to the small business community and changes in the tax system that would be beneficial to small business. Instead, we received a hodge-podge of rehashed promises with the exception of one or two provisions which we were advocating in the first place.
Nevertheless, my primary purpose in taking part in today's debate is to respond to the minister's long awaited announcements. Although it is the duty of the opposition to oppose, as its name implies, the record shows that over the past few years we have been doing much more than that. In matters pertaining to small business we have taken a wide lead in introducing policies and recommendations geared to the small business sector. These measures have proved sound, logical and realistic and have generally been welcomed by small business interest groups and concerned businessmen in every region of Canada.
I shall not repeat here the policies we have introduced in the past due to the lack of time, and because the last time we did so was less than two weeks ago, on May 16, when we took the initiative to introduce again measures to assist the small business community in Canada. In fact, it is ironic, Mr. Speaker, that important as the small business community is, employing well over 50 per cent of the labour force, it has only been the Conservative party which has prompted and initiated debates on small business in the House of Commons. I believe it is this insistence which has moved the government into at least the limited action we witnessed this week.
It seems that the federal sales tax amendments by the Minister of National Revenue were the highlight of the minister's announcements last Tuesday. The proposal is to raise from $10,000 to $50,000 the level of sales by manufacturing firms which would make them exempt from paying the 12 per cent federal sales tax on production and sales.
At first glance this seems like an honourable and welcome gesture by the government. However, does any hon. member here know of a full time manufacturing firm which can operate on total yearly sales of $50,000 a year? We are not talking about small retail outlets, we are talking about manufacturers. Even the government's claim that 11,000 businesses will be affected by this change indicates less than one per cent involvement from the 1.1 million plus small firms operating in Canada today. Less than one per cent, Mr. Speaker, by the government's own admission, and in my opinion less than one tenth of one per cent of full time Canadian manufacturers. That, Mr. Speaker, was the highlight of the minister's announcement when he claimed that this measure will greatly
