enhance the betterment of the over-all small business community in Canada.
I believe consideration should be given instead to removing the federal sales tax from all Canadian owned and operated small business manufacturers. This would not only help the over-all small business community, but make Canadian-produced goods at least competitive with their imported counterparts on which federal sales tax would continue to be collected.
This renewed sense of competition by Canadian manufacturers would naturally stimulate sales and thereby equalize government losses caused by removing the federal sales tax in the first place. This, of course, cannot be done unless a realistic definition is used, one which the government obviously lacks. As I stated last week in this House, the government up to that time had taken four different positions within one year as to definitions, including one of 100 employees or less. Since then a new definition has been added which indicates that a small business is one that has 300 employees or less. In this last definition, as in previous ones, no provisions have been made to exempt subsidiaries of large multinational corporations from the small business definitions.
This latest addition to the government's various definitions only underlines the total chaos within the small business secretariat in its relationship to other federal departments. I repeat that any definition based on the number of employees is only a negative incentive to small business, urging them to curb growth and employment opportunities for the sake of remaining within the small business definition.
We on this side of the House have consistently maintained that the only realistic definition is the one used by the United States small business administration, that being that a small business is one that is owner-managed and not dominant in its field.
The minister also announced that a series of information bulletins will be sent out to small businessmen by his office. Small business does not need more government paperwork. Small business does not need more government directives, regulations or controls. It is obvious that these bulletins would only add to an already heavy paper burden while at the same time promoting the government and the minister himself prior to an election.
One area of importance which the minister did touch on was that of job creation for university graduates. But can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, that the minister is limiting this program to only 800 students, and this on a temporary basis at a cost of $5.4 million to the taxpayer? It is like throwing crumbs at potential voters. What about the thousands of other graduates in Canada who are just as qualified and unable to find job opportunities? At least the minister did not repeat what the Prime Minister told students in Toronto a year or so ago, that if they do not like it here, they should move elsewhere.
I believe that governments, being the largest potential employers in this country by far, should have a set-aside employment program for graduate students along the same lines as a set-aside program for goods and services to small

May 25, 1978
Income Tax Act
business as proposed by my party. In the area of procurement the minister also had an announcement to make. He acknowledged "that small businesses from time to time have cash flow problems which stem from slow payment of bills by the federal government." He promised that progress to speed up these payments will be made. Hurray for the minister! He promised something which should have been done years ago.
The rest of the minister's announcements on Tuesday were generally, as I said at the outset, rehashed policies or proposals already made. For example, the minister emphasized the importance of the Small Businesses Loans Act. This act, Mr. Speaker, has been in effect since 1961 with amendments made last year only for the sake of keeping up with the times. The minister also dwelt on the enterprise development program, for example, and said that millions of dollars are available to small business. No specific number of millions was mentioned though he did say that the amount allocated to the EDP for this coming year is less than last year. And is it really geared to small business? Just recently, the government awarded $8 million to C.C.M., not only a large company on its own but a subsidiary of a multinational corporation, Multi Seaway Corporation. Hardly helpful for small business, is it?
We move now to the second ring of the circus, the minister's tabling of the white paper on venture capital. Yesterday in the House of Commons, after years of persistence by us and other Canadians concerned with the lack of working capital in the small business community, the minister presented a white paper on venture capital. I will not dwell on it very long because most of the paper is dedicated to such sub-titles as "Government recognition of the need to support small business financing". We told the government that years ago. I am happy they finally recognized its importance. In any event, the three basic proposals within the paper are viable to a certain extent although in some cases overlapping with existing programs. The simplest, of course, is to increase the equity investment activities of the FBDB. My own thought is that since the FBDB, an extension of the IDB, has not been overly successful in the past, the idea is perhaps overly simplified.
The second option is to introduce tax measures to enhance the availability of risk capital to small business. This is excellent verbiage except that the paper does not expound on how the government would go about providing these tax measures.
The third option-
Order, please. I suggest the hon. member get back to Bill C-56 and not continue to address himself entirely to the subject of small business.

Mr. Speaker, with all due respect I suggest that Bill C-56 has a great deal to do with small business, tax incentives and with all the other matters connected therewith. If this government-or anyone for that matter-thinks that small business should be disregarded in Bill C-56, it does not have the right perspective of what small business is all about in Canada.
If I may continue, the other option is to introduce tax measures to enhance the availability of risk capital to small business. The option is to create another intermediary vehicle, this time referred to as a venture enterprise company. The bulk of the white paper deals with the licensing requirements of this program, the limitations, ownership, powers and so forth, and generally one can conclude that the incentive to invest in this program is a back end incentive, which would not be very entertaining to the investor. "Back end" means that the incentive would not be there at the beginning, and Canadians would be discouraged from investing in that capital pool. It is obviously based on the United States program called the Small Business Investment Company, operational since 1958; and even the white paper refers to this program as not having been an unqualified success.
Therefore, it seems strange to me that, on the one hand, the government would be considering following the not too successful program of the United States while ignoring the very successful SBA policies, such as the introduction of a small business act or the general definition of small business plus any number of incentive-oriented programs which have been working effectively in the United States.
Although the white paper is impressive in its appearance-it consists of 36 pages-it is far too unrealistic in its recommendations for improving the equity financing environment for small business in Canada. It is, of course, presented for public discussion and therefore all options should stay open, and I do hope it will receive the attention it deserves. In any event, I believe that the recommendations we have been making in this regard, whether we want to call it venture capital, risk capital or working capital, are far more realistic and relatively simple to implement. We must continue to realize that red tape and bureaucracy must be simplified rather than made more complicated. Therefore, one of the ways to increase working capital for small business is to utilize and expand on existing programs.
One such program which is in place but which is under-utilized is the Small Businesses Loans Act, which assists small businesses with sales of $1.5 million or less with up to $75,000 toward fixed assets. My party's recommendation has been to expand this program to include working capital as well, and I will quote from my remarks during our opposition day on Tuesday, May 16. We have been recommending this for quite some time, and we made it clear again that day. I said the following:
-in order to help owner-operated enterprises raise working capital, we are recommending that the small business loans program cover working, as well as investment capital where such funds are not available through normal commercial arrangements. We feel that including working capital assistance within the loans act would enhance the use of the act and assist the small firms where assistance is most required.
This is precisely what the white paper is attempting to achieve, but I am afraid that instead of achieving such an objective it will only enhance the already confusing and contradictory atmosphere which the small business ministry is creating.

May 25, 1978

Our second recommendation in this regard, which we have been advocating for some time, is to provide an incentive tax crecdit to any Canadian citizen who makes a direct investment in the equity of a Canadian-owned small business. This is a front end incentive because the incentive would come to the Canadian citizen directly as a tax credit when investing in a Canadian-owned and Canadian-operated small business enterprise. This again is a typical example of what the white paper is trying to get at. Instead of copying, borrowing, stealing or begging ideas which are available-I do not care which- many of which are operational in the United States and elsewhere, we create a monster, the white paper which was put forward just yesterday in this House for discussion. I hope there will be a discussion of the paper on a national level, but I hope that the final outcome will be simplified and realistic because we need less government and more incentive programs in this very vital sector of our economy.
The third and final tabling of the government was the amendments to the Income Tax Act and the excise tax, which were tabled yesterday. Naturally, we welcome these amendments, particularly the first one which deals with the rollover of capital gains tax to families in small businesses. In March of 1977 we made precisely that recommendation, and I quote: "Amend those provisions of the Income Tax Act which discourage the transfer of small businesses within families or to employees." This tax proposal does do this, but it does not go far enough. There is a limitation of $200,000 and, therefore, as a capital gain only $100,000 is gained.
Second, it does not include employees. In small businesses there are a great number of employees who are close to the ownership, and it would be worthwhile to be able to transfer those businesses to employees rather than shutting them down because the taxes cannot be paid at the time of death.
The other two matters, the capital losses and the amendments to the Income Tax Act, are really just window dressing to the VEIC program proposed in the white paper. We have no objection to that amendment except, as I say, that it is applied by the government to make the VEIC proposal in the white paper more favourable to the investor by amending the Income Tax Act according to the capital losses as outlined in the paper.
The third amendment to the Excise Tax Act by the Minister of National Revenue, through the Minister of Finance, deals strictly with those announcements of last Tuesday on the removal of the federal sales tax for companies whose sales are under $50,000. Basically this last move by the government today in its three-ring circus was clearly just to tie in with the two announcements which were made over the past two days.
It is incredible to me that the latest budget did not include these amendments to the Income Tax Act. Is this a second thought by the government in dealing with small business? Is it because the government has seen fit to move into the small business area after it saw what happened in the Gallup poll? Is it because many people are involved in small business in Canada? It is not that long ago that the budget was introduced, and in fact in the budget-and, to satisfy you, Mr. Income Tax Act
Speaker, in Bill C-56-the limits we are taking off for incorporated farms and farm partnerships as far as the rollovers are concerned do nothing for small business.
Then, as an afterthought, when the government does come in with amendments for the rest of the small business community, they do not compare with the amendments regarding farmers. I agree with those farm amendments. They are long overdue. Farmers deserve the amendments in Bill C-56 and we support them, but why not handle the small business community in a uniform way? Why is there a limit on the other small business sector of our economy? Why are employees not included? These are some of the questions which must be answered by the government in the very near future.
I just want to emphasize that any assistance to small business is naturally welcome. Small business has become, I believe, a partisan issue because everyone always wants to help the small guy. But the government must realize who the small guy is. They cannot make provisions, tax amendments and assistance available in the form of incentive oriented programs unless they come up with a realistic definition of small business. I repeat, we have had five different positions from the government so far as definitions are concerned, and this cannot work. It has not worked in any other industrialized country. Therefore, I recommend again what I have done many times in the House: let us borrow from the United States small business administration their definition of small business which has worked effectively and which is viable. I do not understand why the minister is afraid to come up with that definition rather than changing it every week.
As I said, we welcome as well any policies or measures that the government decides to borrow from us. I say "borrow" because after the next election when we are on the other side we will naturally keep those recommendations and suggestions which we have been making and develop them in such a way that small business will once again become the backbone of our economy, and our economy will once again reflect the healthy and free enterprising system on which this country was built.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to deal with Bill C-56 and I would ask you to be as lenient with me as you have been with the previous speaker. I have always wondered why it was so hard to get along in Canada, particularly Quebec and Ottawa, and now I realize why: Not only do we not speak the same language, Mr. Speaker, but we cannot discuss the same subject.
With regard to Bill C-56, I regret to have to say again that the government has once again brought forward an omnibus bill. This is just another bill designed to make us accept the unacceptable. I think that someday someone will write about this government saying that it was the omnibus bills champion. I think that all the discussions which we have had in this House since the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)
5754

May 25, 1978
Income Tax Act
became the head of the government and most particularly since the issue of the provincial sales tax came up, which will compel us to reject this bill C-56, if the Finance Minister (Mr. Chretien) does not see reason, will have been completely useless if the government won't give way.
The crisis which we are' presently experiencing is just the outcome of the increasingly centralizing policies of this government and if we want to put an end to this rising federal dictature which I have ceaselessly denounced before this House, there is only one way: throw out of this House those intruders into areas of provincial jurisdiction, who are going to destroy Canada. As soon as we rise to defend the constitutional rights of the provinces, and most particularly today, those of Quebec, all the Liberal party tenors call us separatists but where are the separatists actually to be found, Mr. Speaker? Are they not among those who want to strip the provinces of all their powers, which are at the very basis of our Confederation? The Parti Quebecois wants to establish a true and legitimate association so that Canada will cease to have to survive by snatching one compromise after another. With regard to the British North America Act which I do not consider as a constitution but rather a royal decree, do people know that there has never been a formal agreement signed by the Canadian people and supported by it?
All that this act contains is a compromise between the newly constituted provinces of the time and it is from that compromise that have emerged all the struggles between the two founding peoples of Canada, mainly over the past 110 years. England has always acted as the arbitrator between two groups which have never gotten along with one another, because it was actually London's intentions to make us quarrel between ourselves to dominate us. This is what we have never understood in Canada. An in this regard we are not yet decolonized. This is why a petty autocrat such as the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) French by birth and English by principle has managed to bring Canada to the brink of collapse. And just like any dictator has to have its court jester, ours has found one in the person of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who seems to enjoy that role greatly. The Minister of Finance keeps shouting right and left that he does not want to grant Quebec any favors, that he wants to treat the province of Quebec absolutely like any other province. Let us see how he acts out his contradictions. While he accepts to hand over directly to the provincial governments the reimbursement of the loss incurred through cancellation of the sales tax, after entering into various agreements with each one of the provinces, and incidentally those agreements are tailored to the need of each province, when it comes to Quebec, he finds all kinds of reasons not to transfer to the province the amounts he had promised and refuses to allow it the freedom to choose its own mode of taxation and distribution.
This is not the first time the provinces are allowed to choose. It happened with family allowances when Quebec decided on how they would be distributed, contrary to the other provinces; but we did not have then in power the petty dictators we have today. What we have here in this fight is the Prime Minister who, having failed to get the Quebec government to kowtow to him since November 15, 1976 has decided to resort to any legal or illegal means he could find to punish Quebecers for having elected such a government by launching an attack on all sectors of exclusively provincial jurisdiction. Today, he was caught red-handed in the case of the sales tax. Having been found out, he now plays innocent and even proclaims his innocence, laying the blame on the P.Q. government and separatism.
From the very beginning, I have followed the confrontation with regard to the provincial sales tax. Clearly, the present government has once again put its foot in it, not to say in the provinces, by interfering in the field of sales tax which is an area of provincial jurisdiction. We should not forget that. I heard earlier spokesman for the Liberal party say: What is so wrong about that? What is wrong is that you have trampled on someone else's ground and do not want to admit it. To justify this intrusion which all parties in the Quebec national assembly objected to the Minister of Finance tries to flip-flop like the Prime Minister or under his direction.
I do not know exactly how you could call someone who acts exactly contrary to what he preaches. I am not saying he is a liar. Nor is he perfectly honest. In fact, the Minister of Finance is always saying that he does not want to grant the province of Quebec any special privilege and will treat it exactly like any other province. However, in bill C-56 the Minister demonstrates that he deals differently with each province according to the discussions he had privately with each of them except Quebec as they did not accept his proposals like the others. In fact, except Quebec, the other provinces have finally accepted the federal proposal while they reacted and obtained what they asked for as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) mentioned yesterday. And he recognized that the Atlantic provinces were in a position different from that of other provinces. They had different agreements. It appears on page 5695 of the Debates.
First, four provinces have seriously blamed the government, which the Minister does not want to admit, for having invaded an area of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. We must let the people know because the Minister of Finance will not admit it and does not want the people to find out. Second, some provinces asked for a nine months' exemption instead of six months. The federal government has accepted in spite of all the budget difficulties it might cause. Some provinces will have a nine months' cut and for others it will be six months within a twelve months' budget. And last, in the case of some provinces the Minister of Finance has accepted to repay two-thirds of

May 25, 1978

the loss while for other provinces it will be a complete writeoff. And in another province he will pay nothing. The legislation leaves the door open for some other forthcoming arrangements that have yet to be determined. All those provinces had discussions with the minister, and they succeeded in having their requirements accepted according to their criteria. When it comes to Quebec, the finance minister also states his conditions and has priority since it is an exclusively provincial jurisdiction. Although he was extremely surprised to see the federal government invade once more an exclusive jurisdiction of Quebec, Mr. Parizeau listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) make his offer, namely whether he accepted to reduce the sales tax by 3 per cent, the federal government would refund two-thirds of the loss incurred because of this reduction, and the provincial government could get back the 1 per cent through income tax. Although this proposal was against the constitution, Mr. Parizeau accepted it while indicating his preferences or priorities, just as the other provinces did. Here are his priorities: in order to stimulate four industries in the economy of Quebec which had been declining for several years, Mr. Parizeau thought it was time to change direction by removing completely the sales tax in Quebec not for six or nine months, but for twelve months. The government of Quebec and all opposition parties found this proposal fantastic. The Minister of Finance and the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) did not see it that way. Quebec had had the gall to devise a new formula more appropriate to the priorities of the Quebec economy. That is why federal ministers had to punish the Quebec government and all its supporters.
So the Minister of Finance stated that the government of Quebec will not get anything of those $285 million he had for it. But when he found out that all Quebeckers were behind their representatives in the National Assembly and raised a strong protest, the federal minister of Finance then decided to give $285 million directly to taxpayers, that is to those who have filed an income tax return. The minister did not suspect he had made a bigger mistake since he was prepared to make a gift to the rich, forgetting there were 2,500,000 people who are too poor to pay income tax. And he will not gain friends among the millions of taxpayers who filed income tax returns because they know that the provincial government will have to get back that money and all that scheme has been prepared by the federal government. Its last mistake was to refuse to treat Quebec like all the other provinces by forcing it to find the money which the federal government gave to the other provinces.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance believed they had found a way to humiliate the Quebec government but the whole thing boomeranged because the reaction of Quebeckers was quite contrary to what federal liberal party strategists had anticipated. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance succeeded in at least one thing in Quebec, Mr. Income Tax Act
Speaker, that is to achieve unanimity among all parties in the national assembly, among all federal opposition parties and among all Quebeckers who want Quebec to survive and the constitution to be respected. And of course some senators supported the population, unlike federal members who cannot say how they feel about it. Speaking about the flip-flop of the Minister of Finance, I cannot help mentioning the acrobatic trick played by the right hon. Prime Minister on May 18, 1978.
In trying to reply to the question of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), as reported on page 5532 of Hansard:
-yesterday the Prime Minister stated that the same deal on tax room was being offered to all the provinces. I still question that, but the point I want to clarify now is this: will the Prime Minister not concede that the effect of this proposal will be that individuals in the province of Quebec will be affected in a much different way than individuals in the provinces which have agreed to an across-the board reduction in sales tax, and that that effect will be a sort of reverse means test so that in the province of Quebec only those individuals who have income high enough to pay income tax will benefit-
And the Prime Minister replied, and I quote:
-the hon. lady is confusing two things: the federal action and the provincial response. In so far as the federal action is concerned, it is the same in all provinces which accepted the scheme and it is the same in Quebec.
And the Prime Minister went on:
We are cutting taxes and making room so the provinces can increase their income tax ... Obviously what the provinces are delivering is different. Eight of the provinces have said: "Yes,. .. One province has said: "No ... We will cut them in the way we want."
Let us consider the craftiness used by the Prime Minister of Canada to conceal the discrimination he practices against the Quebec government. He attacks the response of the provinces. But surely there are various responses and it could not be otherwise, since the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance contacted them one after the other. Why were they not brought together. It was a matter of national interest since they were going against a basic principle of the constitution. It should have been dealt with at a federal-provincial conference, but when the federal government has infringed upon provincial areas, it has always done so as cunningly as possible. When the Prime Minister states that eight provinces unanimously agreed to the federal proposal, I must point out to him that some of them reacted to the terms and conditions of that proposal, as did Quebec, and it is precisely on that point that I heard recently the Prime Minister expressing his support for the Minister of Finance. It is true that some provinces, after discussions, have accepted a six- or nine-month exemption, but Quebec asked for a 12-month exemption. Why accept six or nine, but not 12? The other provinces indicated that they were primarily interested in a general reduction. Quebec proposed four specific sectors of its economy. I think that Quebec, like the other provinces, had the right to indicate its priorities within its field of taxation.
80038-74^2

May 25, 1978
Income Tax Act
When the Prime Minister says: We are cutting taxes so that the provinces may collect more, I am stunned by such a statement, Mr. Speaker. In my opinion, the Prime Minister should have said: We ask or we suggest that the provinces reduce their sales taxes; instead of we are reducing them. The truth is that the federal government does not cut any of its taxes. It asks the provinces to cut their own taxes. Why let the population believe that the federal government is the most generous? The Minister of Finance wants to punish the province of Quebec because his provincial counterpart took a few weeks before answering to his proposals. Should we not instead blame the federal Minister of Finance for having so long delayed his budget. The two budgets would not have come out at the same time as they did. The Minister of Finance first refused to introduce a budget probably because just before an election he did not want Canadians to realize that it would cost them $56 billion to look after 23 million people. It is a fantastic amount because the government took over all the best tax fields and spends unsparingly, while the provinces cannot find enough money for their administration. The province of Quebec which was preparing its budget as well wanted to know more about the intentions of the federal government in order to gear its own budget accordingly. But because of the budget secrecy and because the government, constantly fears any possible leak I am sure that the Minister of Finance of Quebec had not been informed of some important details, especially when we learn on the side that the Federal government is ready to change the provincial sales tax.
Any serious Minister of Finance would have reacted just as the Quebec Minister did. The federal government ought not to have brought forward generalities, invading somebody else's jurisdiction. If the Minister of Finance had been serious and sincere, he would have gone to Quebec and would have revealed the whole thing to Mr. Parizeau, even at the risk of a few leaks. After all, they are both Ministers of Finance, two Ministers who should be able to keep a secret. One could hardly expect the provincial minister to run after the federal minister because the federal government was asking a favour in coming into a provincial field of jurisdiction to play the good Samaritan. Why did not the government use their own tax fields to bring a tax relief to the people? The federal government has more powers of taxation than the provinces. Why ask the provinces to stimulate the economy when the federal government have all the money?
I am sure that if ever the provinces were to ventures into the federal tax field, this would raise a general outcry here in the House. But with all this quarrelling and more to come, we have an irrefutable evidence of the need for a new Canadian Constitution in order to determine once for all the rights and duties of each level of government, with well defined standards and severe penalties in case of non-compliance.
We have said it time and times again in the House: Canada is made up of various regions; their geography, their various

resources, their economic features make them different. This is why we maintain that not two provinces in Canada are alike and therefore that each of them must be treated differently. That is why we say that a true confederation must be based on the authority of the provinces joined in an economic association, based on a truly Canadian constitution, written for Canadians and voted by Canadians in a referendum, after interprovincial meetings where it will be determined which sectors the provinces wish to relinquish to the federal government which will become the executor of provincial wishes.
It is time, Mr. Speaker, that a group of men from Financial influences took over Canada. Unfortunately today, we are faced with a personality clash where the opponents are risking the future of Canada for their own personal glory. This may surprise everyone, but the minister is showing us here the government's true face.
Since this Prime Minister has been leading the government, he has been dreaming of the day he has all fiscal rights now enjoyed by the provinces. He is dreaming of a central government for Canada, and yesterday we heard the statement made by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) on the subject. I believe it perfectly reflects this government's schemes. Let me quote his comments from page 5699 of Hansard'.
... One could even accuse me of being a centralist. I do not mind that, because I believe that in order to hold this nation together we have to accept the fact that there should be one government for the whole of the nation.
That is the Liberal party's dream, Mr. Speaker. Those are the people who pretend to save Confederation, who do not even realize they are destroying it. All those centralist federalists must have read the sad history of federal-provincial conferences, which shows all the tricks used by various Liberal governments to steal tax fields away from the provinces in order to completely dominate them one day.
A single scenario runs through all those conferences. The federal government takes hold of the most profitable tax fields, leaving only residues for the provinces, and then perforce remitting them a share to allow them to survive, rebating a fraction after they have taken everything. Or alternately, the federal makes loans, this is still better, loans that tie them up, ropes around their necks, those famous shared cost programs that are just so many ropes to hold the provinces and make them pay interest to the federal government.
Repay five for one!

A province with a five to ten year loan repays five and ten times the principal. In the 1867 financial arrangements, it is stated that the federal gets unlimited taxing powers in indirect taxes, but direct taxes were so hated it left them to provinces. Anything repugnant was left to the provinces.
With changing direct taxation, especially in the 40's, the provinces had to enter direct taxation because the federal
May 25, 1978

government had occupied everything else. When direct taxation became profitable for the provinces, especially in the 40's, the federal government used all available tricks to get its hands on direct taxes, because he saw they were profitable, to the dismay of the provinces losing the main bulkwork of their autonomy.
As the government of that time could not get the agreement of the provinces, the Minister of Finance used its discretionary powers in wartime to declare that the dominion would levy taxes on personal and corporate income. It forced the provinces to find other sources of revenue, which explains the series of small taxes that the provinces had to levy while the federal government used those additional revenues to invade areas under provincial jurisdiction such as health, education, municipal affairs, because the provinces no longer had the money to work in those fields. That is the federal government's iron collar of which we have been trying to rid ourselves since this famous invasion.
And again today, after they robbed the provinces of their direct taxation power, they have the nerve to propose the abolition of the provincial revenue department. The Minister of Finance declared that if Quebec considers it too expensive, they should abolish their revenue department. They go really far. They even went further by creating a federal Department of Urban Affairs. This is the most serious insult, everybody knows that towns and municipalities are strictly under provincial jurisdiction.
Not satisfied with having its own Department of Agriculture, its own Department of Labour, its own Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, its Department of Communications, its Department of Fisheries and Environment, its Department of Regional Economic Expansion, its Department of National Flealth, the federal government has now created its own Department of Urban Affairs. All of these already exist at the provincial level, but the federal government wants to play the same role as the provinces in Canada. As I watched the right hon. Prime Minister in the last few years, and more recently the Minister of Finance, I have been wondering if they have not sworn to destroy Canada and if their prejudices against Quebec did not override every other consideration. The survival of Canada should not be based on the result of a confrontation between two men.
National interests outweigh the pride of a few politicians who seem to care nothing about better harmony among our provinces. I only hope that what I said here tonight will bring back to sanity certain Liberal party leaders who seem to ignore the law, the constitutional agreements and show no respect for the provinces and cannot forget about their resentment for Quebeckers because they elected that particular government on November 15, 1976. The bitterness has reached its climax with that surprising interference of the Minister of Finance in a tax field which has always been recognized as being exclusive to Quebec. And still more recently, the latest statements
Adjournment Debate
made by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouel-let), thus following the example of his leader, the Minister of Finance and others. It so happens that the little people in Quebec have succeeded in reaching a consensus in Quebec, something that not one government had managed to do since Confederation, to alienate all parties in Quebec.
I heard Mr. Gerard D. Levesque, Mr. Claude Ryan, Mr. Goldbloom state on television that they strongly objected to the statements of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. I sincerely hope that all those testimonies will bring the Minister of Finance to his senses and that he will refrain from shirking the issue and from playing on words about the the rebate to Quebec. He may not like the PQ supporters, but he should not forget that most Quebeckers of all political parties do not like at all the present Minister of Finance.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I wonder if you would call it ten o'clock and not count this as my time to speak? I cannot speak tomorrow and I would like to speak next week.
Shall we call it ten o'clock?
Agreed.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: CANADA COUNCIL-REQUEST MANDATE BE STUDIED BY COMMITTEE
CANADA COUNCIL-REQUEST MANDATE BE STUDIED BY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I made my motion back in early April suggesting that the House of Commons should assign the committee on broadcasting and the arts to re-examine the mandate of the Canada Council, the minister received the request in a careful, studied and seemingly concerned manner and indicated that he would look into the matter. That was the first time he had said in his studied way that he would look at the matter. Well, he looked at the matter. Then he looked at the matter six months ago when I raised it and I thought, "Well, I shall raise it again in the House of Commons". This is that opportunity.
However, as I stand to raise this issue I know that the minister has already answered. In fact, he gave the studied, careful response that he would make in an address to the



May 25, 1978
Adjournment Debate
Canadian Conference of the Arts in Halifax on April 28. That studied response in reference to the arts and their relationship to the Canada Council and its relationship to the government was entitled "The Relationship between Government and Support for the Arts". I waited anticipating that we might have a response, even a non-partisan look at the Canada Council mandate, the Canada Council's relationship to government, members of parliament and the people of Canada. And what was the response? It was one of the most amazing and irresponsible speeches that I have heard given by a minister.
I could understand when he stood up in this House of Commons and in committee and said, "I am not accountable or responsible for the Canada Council." The Canada Council agreed he was not responsible. So who was responsible and accountable? We were led to believe it was this House of Commons-you and me, Mr. Speaker. If we are going to be responsible, I say let us look at the information. Let us look at the criticisms of the Auditor General who said that things were not right in the Canada Council; that in the way they were spending their money there was not adequate invoicing, there was not adequate documentation, there was not adequate assessment. It was one of the severest criticisms in the Auditor General's report.
In reply to the allegations of the Auditor General the Canada Council has said, "Mr. Auditor General, you are overstating the matter. It is just not so." Now we have a dispute between the Auditor General and the Canada Council, each of them saying very opposite things on the basis of some documentation. One of them is saying that this is serious and the other one is saying that it is not. Mr. Speaker, who is to judge whether the allegations of the Auditor General are serious? The minister cannot be the judge.
In committee I asked if he had access to the files of the Canada Council and his answer was that he did not. He has confirmed that in his speech. Can you believe a minister would make a statement such as the following:
Politicians, on both the opposition and government sides of the Commons, have been demanding information-
What a terrible thing, that members of the House of Commons should be demanding information, Mr. Speaker! The minister continued:
I am not one of them. I want to be clear about that.
Then he went on in the next paragraph to say:
I am opposed to that. So long as I am Secretary of State I shall not allow interference-
I want to give notice tonight to this House of Commons, to the minister, to parliament and to the people of Canada that I intend to interfere, and my interference is just starting. I realize now how absolutely necessary it is that I interfere, because the minister refuses to accept his responsibility. In addition to that his attitude is that, if he is not going to do it, then members of parliament will have to.

I should like to give the House the minister's description of himself, Mr. Speaker-not my description or that of another person eulogizing him. This is what he said in the same speech:
I regard myself, personally, as a sensitive and discriminating individual, knowledgeable of our past cultural heritage, perceptive, and sure of what should or should not be accepted. I am quite assertive and combative about my judgments:
I hold to them strongly. I am undismayed by the fact that few agree with me. I am superbly confident of my taste.
That is the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) speaking of himself. He is a paragon, Mr. Speaker. But what does this very sure person do with what he has? I will quote him again:
Politicians, on both the opposition and government sides of the Commons, have been demanding information-
And then again:
I am not one of them.
In the House I asked the minister if he had ever been refused information by the Canada Council.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-COMPENSATION FOR LOSSES INCURRED IN SINKING OF "WILLIAM CARSON"

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: TRANSPORT-COMPENSATION FOR LOSSES INCURRED IN SINKING OF "WILLIAM CARSON"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in connection with a question I asked of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) yesterday about the sinking of the William Carson and his reaction to some things that now need to be clarified. I received an unsatisfactory response. In fact, I did not get much of a response at all.
The Minister of Transport, as all members know, is as popular as a school of dogfish in a cod trap. He is continuing to sully his reputation in that direction. In fact, today in the transport committee it was moved that the committee does not have any confidence in the Minister of Transport and urges the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to request his resignation, a motion I would strongly support.
On May 23 the minister made public the report of Mr. Justice Nathaniel S. Noel of the Newfoundland Supreme Court on his investigation into the sinking of the m.v. William Carson off Labrador, on June 3, 1977. By the way, that report is dated January 27. The minister explained today that he did not receive it until March 13. Well, even March 13 is 71 days earlier than May 23. Why did the public have to wait 71 days to have the minister make this public? It is unjustified. It should have been made public a lot sooner. It does not take 71 days to print this little report that I have in my hand now.
The commissioner found that the vessel sank, and I quote:
-due to the default of the vessel's operator, Canadian National Railway Company and her Master, Norman Lewis Hinks, the sinking was caused by ice penetrating the hull when the vessel was making a passage through an ice field on a voyage from St. Anthony to Cartwright.
Adjournment Debate
At the end of his report he repeats those findings. I quote from page 39:
The sinking of the m.v. William Carson was contributed to by the default of her Master, Norman Lewis Hinks, who directed the ship into the hazards of Labrador ice when there was no grave necessity to do so.
At page 40 he states:
The sinking of the m.v. William Carson was contributed to by the default of her operators, Canadian National Railway Company, who sent the ship on a voyage to Goose Bay, via intermediate ports, when it was known and intended that she would encounter Labrador ice, under a Master who had little experience in the conditions to be met.
Mr. Justice Noel may be right or not right in his conclusions and opinions, but this is what he has found after studying the case. This brings up several questions. One that arises is whether CN, who are not going to be pleased with this report of Mr. Justice Noel, and I cannot blame them, will be driven by the conclusions of this report perhaps to hesitate to send a ship up to Goose Bay this year while there is still Labrador ice around. The Bond is supposed to replace the Carson and is to be under way on July 4. It is possible CN will say they are not going to send a ship, that they will not take that responsibility in view of this report.
I asked the minister today in that committee what he would do in that event. It is possible CN might say: "We are not going to send a ship; we are not going to take responsibility in view of this report". I asked the minister today in committee what would he do in that event. He seemed to indicate there was only one course of action to take. The government would then have to instruct CN to send a vessel or to agree to indemnify them and take the responsibility to assure that that service starts as soon as possible, that the people on the Labrador coast get the cargo and other supplies they need and enjoy the passenger service that is required. I hope the minister understands this and that if CN attempts this manoeuvre he will counteract it immediately.
Yesterday I asked him:
Is he going to direct the CNR to pay the passengers and crew loss claims and the cargo owners their claims which have been in abeyance now for 11 months?
There were 1,000 tons of cargo aboard the vessel, Mr. Speaker. It was not insured by the consignees. It was not insured by CN. CN, a Crown corporation, has refused to pay the claims. It will be 12 months one week from Saturday, on June 3, 1978, during which the cargo owners have had to sustain this cost not knowing whether they will ever be paid.
Canadian National has stated that the claims will only be paid if the company is held legally liable. CN has certainly been found, now, to be liable by the commissioner, Mr. Justice Noel, so I asked the minister where he would now direct the railway company to pay up with no further delay. Some of these small businesses in Labrador are in a bankrupt condition. It was the start of the season last year when the Carson sank, and very large consignments were on the way to them. The minister said:

May 25, 1978
Adjournment Debate
It would not be my intention to give directions to the Canadian National. I am sure they are looking at their legal position and what is their proper course of action.
Mr. Speaker, the government is responsible for this service. The government meets its deficits through subsidies. The minister can direct CN. It is the government that is responsible. The minister should say to CN: "Pay those cargo owners. Never mind your strict legal liability, never mind running them through the courts for the next three or four years, pay up; we have a commission report that says you were in default." But he has given no undertaking he would do this.
Then when I asked him whether he would have CN speed the matter up, he said:
I would certainly be glad if I could do anything to speed up the resolution of the questions referred to in the first part of the hon. member's question.
What nonsense, saying he would be glad if he could speed it up. That is no answer. He is the minister. He could order the company on behalf of the government to settle these claims or to speed up the settlement.
Then I asked him whether the government was going to take action against the CN to recover the value of the Carson which had been lost due to fault on the part of the company. The minister replied:
The Canadian National was operating this vessel on behalf of the government and I would want to have legal advice as to the implications of that in respect of any potential claim.
It is time, Mr. Speaker, for this minister to wake up and observe his responsibilities. Here are those poor cargo owners, 1,000 tons of cargo lost, and their claims are still not peid. It may take years for the courts to settle this. Mr. Justice Noel has given his view and opinion now. Why should the vast CN Crown corporation be able to punish them by making them wait for years for their money? Or perhaps they won't get it at all in strict legal terms.

I suggest that at least the first half of the question he asked tonight is neither of those two species but probably herring of the red variety. Having spent a lot of time on the first question he raised with the minister with respect particularly to the date of January 27, he today finds out that he was wrong about that date, so the next tack is to say that, notwithstanding what the time was, it still has been too long. He emphasized that the date, which he now admits was March-I think March 9-was still too long ago.
The essence and the crunch of what the hon. member is getting to is the fact that he would have the minister direct CN to pay. I suggest that the hon. member ask us to direct Canadian National to pay compensation to those who lost goods as a result of the sinking. In so doing he would have us pre-empt the legal process, and I do not think he really means that. Perhaps he really has not thought about it. In any event, I believe that all hon. members sympathize with those who are in this position. However, surely the hon. member would not want the government to act arbitrarily in this case in setting aside the legal rights which exist not only for the company but for the claimants as well.
With regard to the whole question of claims I can do no more than reiterate what the minister has said, that CN should deal with the situation expeditiously and with the sensitivity which is always appropriate for any business in a situation like this involving many individual claims.
